docstring:
The three-dimensional case, proved by Wang, Zahl [WaZa25].

[WaZa25] Wang, H. and Zahl, J., _Volume estimates for unions of convex sets, and the Kakeya set conjecture in three dimensions_. arXiv preprint, arXiv:2502.17655, 2025.
statement: Kakeya.KakeyaSetConjectureDim 3

docstring:
The Pierce-Birkhoff conjecture holds for `n = 1`.
This was proved by Louis Mahé.
statement:
∀ (f : ℝ → ℝ),
  PierceBirkhoff.IsPiecewisePolynomial f →
    ∃ ι κ g, Finite ι ∧ Finite κ ∧ ∀ (x : ℝ), f x = ⨆ i, ⨅ j, Polynomial.eval x (g i j)

docstring:
The Pierce-Birkhoff conjecture holds for `n = 2`.
This was proved by Louis Mahé.
statement:
∀ (f : (Fin 2 → ℝ) → ℝ),
  PierceBirkhoff.IsPiecewiseMvPolynomial f →
    ∃ ι κ g, Finite ι ∧ Finite κ ∧ ∀ (x : Fin 2 → ℝ), f x = ⨆ i, ⨅ j, (MvPolynomial.eval x) (g i j)

docstring:
The Pierce-Birkhoff conjecture states that for every real piecewise-polynomial function
`f : ℝⁿ → ℝ`, there exists a finite set of polynomials `gᵢⱼ ∈ ℝ[x₁, ..., xₙ]` such that
`f = supᵢ infⱼ(gᵢⱼ)`.
statement:
∀ {n : ℕ} (f : (Fin n → ℝ) → ℝ),
  PierceBirkhoff.IsPiecewiseMvPolynomial f →
    ∃ ι κ g, Finite ι ∧ Finite κ ∧ ∀ (x : Fin n → ℝ), f x = ⨆ i, ⨅ j, (MvPolynomial.eval x) (g i j)

docstring:
Given any set of $n$ complex numbers $\{z_1, ..., z_n\}$ that are linearly independent over
$\mathbb{Q}$, the field extension $\mathbb{Q}(z_1, ..., z_n, e^{z_1}, ..., e^{z_n})$
has transcendence degree at least $n$ over $\mathbb{Q}$.
statement:
∀ (n : ℕ) (z : Fin n → ℂ),
  LinearIndependent ℚ z →
    have hinj := ⋯;
    ↑n ≤ Algebra.trdeg ℚ ↥(IntermediateField.adjoin ℚ (Set.range z ∪ Set.range (Complex.exp ∘ z)))

docstring:
A Lucas–Wieferich prime associated with $(a,b)$ is an odd prime $p$, not dividing $a^2 - b$, such
that $U_{p-\varepsilon}(a,b) \equiv 0 \pmod{p^2}$ where $U(a,b)$ is the Lucas sequence of the first
kind and $\varepsilon$ is the Legendre symbol $\left({\tfrac {a^2-4b}{p}}\right)$.
The discriminant of this number is the quantity $a^2 - 4b$. It is conjectured that there are
infinitely many Lucas–Wieferich primes of any given discriminant.
statement: ∀ {D : ℕ}, 0 < D → D ≡ 0 [MOD 4] ∨ D ≡ 1 [MOD 4] → {p | ∃ a b, a ^ 2 - 4 * b = D ∧ IsLucasWieferichPrime a b p}.Infinite

docstring:
A prime $p$ is a Wall–Sun–Sun prime if and only if $L_p \equiv 1 \pmod{p^2}$, where $L_p$ is the
$p$-th Lucas number. It is conjectured that there are infinitely many Wall-Sun-Sun primes.
statement: {p | IsWallSunSunPrime p}.Infinite

docstring:
A prime $p$ is a Wall–Sun–Sun prime if and only if $L_p \equiv 1 \pmod{p^2}$, where $L_p$ is the
$p$-th Lucas number. It is conjectured that there is at least one Wall–Sun–Sun prime.
statement: ∃ p, IsWallSunSunPrime p

docstring:
The following tighter bound depending on the degree $d$ of the polynomial $p$,
in the case of $p$ all roots having the same norm has been shown by Tischler.
$|p(z) - p(c)|/|z-c| \le (d-1)/d \cdot |p'(z)|$.
statement:
∀ (p : Polynomial ℂ),
  2 ≤ p.natDegree →
    (∀ (x y : ℂ), p.IsRoot x ∧ p.IsRoot y → ‖x‖ = ‖y‖) →
      ∀ (z : ℂ) (K : ℝ),
        ∃ c,
          Polynomial.eval c (Polynomial.derivative p) = 0 ∧
            ‖Polynomial.eval z p - Polynomial.eval c p‖ / ‖z - c‖ ≤
              (↑p.natDegree - 1) / ↑p.natDegree * ‖Polynomial.eval z (Polynomial.derivative p)‖

docstring:
Given a complex polynomial $p$ of degree $d ≥ 2$ and a complex number $z$
there is a critical point $c$ of $p$, such that $|p(z)-p(c)|/|z-c| ≤ |p'(z)|$.
statement:
∀ (p : Polynomial ℂ),
  2 ≤ p.degree →
    ∀ (z : ℂ) (K : ℝ),
      ∃ c,
        Polynomial.eval c (Polynomial.derivative p) = 0 ∧
          ‖Polynomial.eval z p - Polynomial.eval c p‖ / ‖z - c‖ ≤ ‖Polynomial.eval z (Polynomial.derivative p)‖

docstring:
The following weaker version of the mean value problem has been proven.
Given a complex polynomial $p$ of degree $d ≥ 2$ and a complex number $z$
there a critical point $c$ of $p$, such that $|p(z)-p(c)|/|z-c| ≤ 4|p'(z)|$.
statement:
∀ (p : Polynomial ℂ),
  2 ≤ p.degree →
    ∀ (z : ℂ) (K : ℝ),
      ∃ c,
        Polynomial.eval c (Polynomial.derivative p) = 0 ∧
          ‖Polynomial.eval z p - Polynomial.eval c p‖ / ‖z - c‖ ≤ 4 * ‖Polynomial.eval z (Polynomial.derivative p)‖

docstring:
The following tighter bound depending on the degree $d$ of the polynomial $p$,
in the case of $p$ only having real roots has been shown by Tischler.
$|p(z)-p(c)|/|z-c| \le (d-1)/d \cdot |p'(z)|$
statement:
∀ (p : Polynomial ℂ),
  2 ≤ p.natDegree →
    (∀ (x : ℂ), p.IsRoot x → x.im = 0) →
      ∀ (z : ℂ) (K : ℝ),
        ∃ c,
          Polynomial.eval c (Polynomial.derivative p) = 0 ∧
            ‖Polynomial.eval z p - Polynomial.eval c p‖ / ‖z - c‖ ≤
              (↑p.natDegree - 1) / ↑p.natDegree * ‖Polynomial.eval z (Polynomial.derivative p)‖

docstring: Weak form of Hall's conjecture: relax the exponent from $1/2$ to $1/2 - \varepsilon$.
statement: ∀ ε > 0, Hall.HallConjectureExp (2⁻¹ - ε)

docstring:
Elkies' example $(x, y) = (5853886516781223, 447884928428402042307918)$ shows that such $C$ must be
less than $0.0215$. Note that simple `linarith` does not work here.
statement: ∀ (C : ℝ), Hall.HallIneq C 2⁻¹ → C < 215e-4

docstring:
Danilov proved that one cannot replace the exponent $1/2$ with larger number.
In other words, for any $\delta > 0$, there is no positive constant $C$ such that
$|y^2 - x^3| > C |x| ^ {1/2 + \delta}$ for all integers $x, y$ with $y^2 \ne x^3$.
statement: ∀ δ > 0, ¬Hall.HallConjectureExp (2⁻¹ + δ)

docstring: Original Hall's conjecture with exponent $1/2$.
statement: Hall.HallConjectureExp 2⁻¹

docstring: `μ=M(X^10 + X^9 - X^7 - X^6 - X^5 - X^4 - X^3 + X + 1)` is the best value for `lehmer_mahler_measure_problem`.
statement:
∀ (f : Polynomial ℤ),
  LehmerMahlerMeasureProblem.mahlerMeasureZ f > 1 →
    LehmerMahlerMeasureProblem.mahlerMeasureZ f ≥
      LehmerMahlerMeasureProblem.mahlerMeasureZ LehmerMahlerMeasureProblem.lehmerPolynomial

docstring: If $f$ is not reciprocal and $M(f) > 1$ then $M(f) \ge M(X^3 - X - 1)$.
statement:
∀ (f : Polynomial ℤ),
  LehmerMahlerMeasureProblem.mahlerMeasureZ f > 1 →
    f.reverse ≠ f →
      LehmerMahlerMeasureProblem.mahlerMeasureZ f ≥
        LehmerMahlerMeasureProblem.mahlerMeasureZ (Polynomial.X ^ 3 - Polynomial.X - 1)

docstring:
Let `M(f)` denote the Mahler measure of `f`.
There exists a constant `μ>1` such that for any `f(x)∈ℤ[x], M(f)>1 → M(f)≥μ`.
statement:
∃ μ,
  ∀ (f : Polynomial ℤ),
    μ > 1 ∧ (LehmerMahlerMeasureProblem.mahlerMeasureZ f > 1 → LehmerMahlerMeasureProblem.mahlerMeasureZ f ≥ μ)

docstring: If all the coefficients of $f$ are odd and $M(f) > 1$, then $M(f) \ge M(X^2 - X - 1)$.
statement:
∀ (f : Polynomial ℤ),
  LehmerMahlerMeasureProblem.mahlerMeasureZ f > 1 →
    LehmerMahlerMeasureProblem.Polynomial.HasOddCoeffs f →
      LehmerMahlerMeasureProblem.mahlerMeasureZ f ≥
        LehmerMahlerMeasureProblem.mahlerMeasureZ (Polynomial.X ^ 2 - Polynomial.X - 1)

docstring: The **Köthe conjecture**: every left nil radical is contained in the Köthe radical.
statement: ∀ {R : Type u_1} [inst : Ring R] {I : Ideal R}, Koethe.IsNil I → ↑I ⊆ ↑(Koethe.KotheRadical R)

docstring:
The **Amitsur Conjecture**: If `J` is a nil ideal in `R`, then `J[x]` is a nil ideal of the polynomial ring `R[x]`.
This is known to be false, see Agata Smoktunowicz, _Polynomial rings over nil rings need not be nil_.
statement: ∀ {R : Type u_1} [inst : Ring R] (J : TwoSidedIdeal R), Koethe.IsNil J → Koethe.IsNil (TwoSidedIdeal.map Polynomial.C J)

docstring: The **Köthe conjecture**: for any positive integer `n`, the Köthe radical of `R` is the matrix ideal `M_2(Nil*(R))`.
statement:
∀ {R : Type u_1} [inst : Ring R] {I : TwoSidedIdeal R},
  Koethe.IsNil I →
    ∀ (n : Type u_2) [inst_1 : Fintype n],
      TwoSidedIdeal.matrix n (Koethe.KotheRadical R) = Koethe.KotheRadical (Matrix n n R)

docstring: The **Köthe conjecture**: In any ring, the sum of two nil left ideals is nil.
statement: ∀ {R : Type u_1} [inst : Ring R] (I J : Ideal R), Koethe.IsNil I → Koethe.IsNil J → Koethe.IsNil (I + J)

docstring:
The **Köthe conjecture**: for any nil ideal `I` of `R`, the matrix ideal `M_2(I)` is a nil ideal
of the matrix ring `M_2(R)`.
statement: ∀ {R : Type u_1} [inst : Ring R] {I : TwoSidedIdeal R}, Koethe.IsNil I → Koethe.IsNil (TwoSidedIdeal.matrix (Fin 2) I)

docstring:
The **Köthe conjecture**: for any nil ideal `I` of `R`, the matrix ideal `M_n(I)` is a nil ideal
of the matrix ring `M_n(R)`.
statement:
∀ {R : Type u_1} [inst : Ring R] {I : TwoSidedIdeal R},
  Koethe.IsNil I → ∀ (n : Type u_2) [inst_1 : Fintype n], Koethe.IsNil (TwoSidedIdeal.matrix n I)

docstring: Does there exist a point in the plane at rational distance from all four vertices of the unit square?
statement: True ↔ ∃ P, ∀ (i : Fin 4), ¬Irrational (dist P (RationalDistanceProblem.UnitSquareCorners i))

docstring: If Mahler's conjecture is true, i.e. there are no Z-numbers, then `Ω(3/2)` exceeds `1/2`.
statement: (∀ (x : ℝ), x ≠ 0 → Mahler32.IsZNumber x → False) → 1 / 2 < Mahler32.Ω (3 / 2)

docstring: It is known that for all rational `p/q > 1` in lowest terms, we have `Ω(p/q) > 1/p`.
statement: ∀ (p q : ℕ), 1 < q → p.Coprime q → q < p → 1 / ↑p < Mahler32.Ω (↑p / ↑q)

docstring: The **Mahler Conjecture** states that there are no non-zero Z-numbers.
statement: ∀ (x : ℝ), x ≠ 0 → Mahler32.IsZNumber x → False

docstring:
**Four exponentials conjecture**
Let $x_0, x_1$ and $y_0, y_1$ be $\mathbb Q$-linearly independent pairs of complex numbers,
then some $e^{x_i y_j}$ is transcendental.
statement: ∀ (x y : Fin 2 → ℂ), LinearIndependent ℚ x → LinearIndependent ℚ y → ∃ i j, Transcendental ℚ (Complex.exp (x i * y j))

docstring:
The four exponential conjecture would imply that for any irrational number $t$,
at least one of the numbers $2^t$ and $3^t$ is transcendental.
statement: ∀ (t : ℝ), Irrational t → Transcendental ℚ (2 ^ t) ∨ Transcendental ℚ (3 ^ t)

docstring:
Does there exist a composite number $n > 1$ such that Euler’s totient function
$\varphi(n)$ divides $n - 1$?
statement: True ↔ ∃ n > 1, ¬Prime n ∧ n.totient ∣ n - 1

docstring:
**Schinzel conjecture (H hypothesis)**
If a finite set of polynomials $f_i$ satisfies both Schinzel and Bunyakovsky conditions,
there exist infinitely many natural numbers $n$ such that $f_i(n)$ are primes for all $i$.
$e + \pi$ is transcendental.
statement: Transcendental ℚ (Real.exp 1 + Real.pi)

docstring: At least one of Catalan constant and the Gompertz constant is transcendental.
statement: Transcendental ℚ catalanConstant ∨ Transcendental ℚ gompertzConstant

docstring: The Gompertz constant $\delta$ is transcendental.
statement: Transcendental ℚ gompertzConstant

docstring:
$\Gamma(1/4)$ is transcendental.

[Ch84] Chudnovsky, G. (1984). Contributions to the theory of transcendental numbers.
statement: Transcendental ℚ (Real.Gamma (1 / 4))

docstring:
$\pi^{\pi^{\pi^\pi}}$ is not an integer.

This would follow from $\pi^{\pi^{\pi^\pi}}$ being transcendental,
but this formulation is of interest in its own right,
as it could in principle be proven by direct computation.

*Reference:* [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BdHFLfv-ThQ)
statement: ¬∃ n, Real.pi ^ Real.pi ^ Real.pi ^ Real.pi = ↑n

docstring: $\sin(e)$ is transcendental.
statement: Transcendental ℚ (Real.sin (Real.exp 1))

docstring: $\log(\pi)$ is transcendental.
statement: Transcendental ℚ (Real.log Real.pi)

docstring: $e^{\pi^2}$ is transcendental.
statement: Transcendental ℚ (Real.exp (Real.pi ^ 2))

docstring: $\pi^e$ is transcendental.
statement: Transcendental ℚ (Real.pi ^ Real.exp 1)

docstring: $\pi^{\pi^{\pi^\pi}}$ is transcendental.
statement: Transcendental ℚ (Real.pi ^ Real.pi ^ Real.pi ^ Real.pi)

docstring: The Catalan constant $G$ is transcendental.
statement: Transcendental ℚ catalanConstant

docstring:
$\Gamma(1/6)$ is transcendental.

[Ch84] Chudnovsky, G. (1984). Contributions to the theory of transcendental numbers.
statement: Transcendental ℚ (Real.Gamma (1 / 6))

docstring: $\log(\log(2))$ is transcendental.
statement: Transcendental ℚ (Real.log (Real.log 2))

docstring: $e^e$ is transcendental.
statement: Transcendental ℚ (Real.exp (Real.exp 1))

docstring: $\pi^{\sqrt{2}}$ is transcendental.
statement: Transcendental ℚ (Real.pi ^ √2)

docstring:
$\Gamma(1/3)$ is transcendental.

[Ch84] Chudnovsky, G. (1984). Contributions to the theory of transcendental numbers.
statement: Transcendental ℚ (Real.Gamma (1 / 3))

docstring: At least one of $\pi + e$ and $\pi e$ is transcendental.
statement: Transcendental ℚ (Real.pi + Real.exp 1) ∨ Transcendental ℚ (Real.pi * Real.exp 1)

docstring: $\Gamma(1/n)$ for `n ≥ 2` is transcendental.
statement: ∀ (n : ℕ), 2 ≤ n → Transcendental ℚ (Real.Gamma (1 / ↑n))

docstring: $e\pi$ is transcendental.
statement: Transcendental ℚ (Real.exp 1 * Real.pi)

docstring: $\pi^{\pi}$ is transcendental.
statement: Transcendental ℚ (Real.pi ^ Real.pi)

docstring: $\pi^{\pi^{\pi}}$ is transcendental.
statement: Transcendental ℚ (Real.pi ^ Real.pi ^ Real.pi)

docstring:
$\Gamma(1/2)$ is transcendental.

[Ch84] Chudnovsky, G. (1984). Contributions to the theory of transcendental numbers.
statement: Transcendental ℚ (Real.Gamma (1 / 2))

docstring:
The pebbling number conjecture:
the pebbling number of a Cartesian product of graphs is at most equal to the product of the
pebbling numbers of the factors.
statement:
∀ {V : Type} [inst : DecidableEq V] [inst_1 : Fintype V] (G H : SimpleGraph V),
  PebblingNumberConjecture.PebblingNumber (G □ H) ≤
    PebblingNumberConjecture.PebblingNumber G * PebblingNumberConjecture.PebblingNumber H

∀ {V : Type} [inst : DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) (A : PebblingNumberConjecture.PebbleDistribution V),
  PebblingNumberConjecture.IsReachable G A A

∀ {V : Type} [inst : DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) (A : PebblingNumberConjecture.PebbleDistribution V) {v w : V},
  2 ≤ A v →
    G.Adj v w →
      PebblingNumberConjecture.IsPebblingMove G A fun u => if u = w then A u + 1 else if u = v then A u - 2 else A u

docstring: The pebbling number of the complete graph on `n` vertices is `n`.
statement:
∀ {V : Type} [inst : DecidableEq V] [inst_1 : Fintype V],
  PebblingNumberConjecture.PebblingNumber (SimpleGraph.completeGraph V) = Fintype.card V

docstring:
**The zero-divisor conjecture**

If `G` is torsion-free, then the group algebra `K[G]` has no non-trivial zero divisors.
statement:
∀ (K : Type u_1) [inst : Field K] (G : Type u_2) [inst_1 : Group G],
  IsMulTorsionFree G → NoZeroDivisors (MonoidAlgebra K G)

docstring: If $P$ is the Promislow group, then the group ring $\mathbb{C}[P]$ has a non-trivial unit.
statement: ∃ u, ¬Kaplansky.IsTrivialUnit ↑u

∀ (K : Type u_1) [inst : Field K] (G : Type u_2) [inst_1 : Group G] {u : MonoidAlgebra K G},
  Kaplansky.IsTrivialUnit u → IsUnit u

docstring: The Promislow group is torsion-free.
statement: IsMulTorsionFree Kaplansky.PromislowGroup

docstring: There is a counterexample to **Unit Conjecture** in any characteristic.
statement:
∀ (p : ℕ),
  p = 0 ∨ Nat.Prime p → ∃ G x, ∃ (_ : IsMulTorsionFree G), ∃ K x_2, ∃ (_ : CharP K p), ∃ u, ¬Kaplansky.IsTrivialUnit ↑u

docstring:
**The idempotent conjecture**

If `G` is torsion-free, then `K[G]` has no non-trivial idempotents.
statement:
∀ (K : Type u_1) [inst : Field K] (G : Type u_2) [inst_1 : Group G],
  IsMulTorsionFree G → ∀ (a : MonoidAlgebra K G), IsIdempotentElem a → a = 0 ∨ a = 1

docstring: If $P$ is the Promislow group, then the group ring $\mathbb{F}_p[P]$ has a non-trivial unit.
statement: ∀ (p : ℕ) [hp : Fact (Nat.Prime p)], ∃ u, ¬Kaplansky.IsTrivialUnit ↑u

docstring:
The **Unit Conjecture** is false.

At least there is a counterexample for any prime and zero characteristic:
[Mu21] Murray, A. (2021). More Counterexamples to the Unit Conjecture for Group Rings.
[Pa21] Passman, D. (2021). On the counterexamples to the unit conjecture for group rings.
[Ga24] Gardam, G. (2024). Non-trivial units of complex group rings.
statement:
∃ G x,
  ∃ (_ : IsMulTorsionFree G),
    ∀ (p : ℕ), p = 0 ∨ Nat.Prime p → ∃ K x_3, ∃ (_ : CharP K p), ∃ u, ¬Kaplansky.IsTrivialUnit ↑u

docstring:
The first Cuboid conjecture

The DeepMind prover agent has found a formal disproof of this statement.

An (independent) informal solution can be found here:
*Reference:* [arxiv/2510.11768](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.11768) **Irreducibility of the Cuboid Polynomial P_{a,u}(t) via a Rank-Zero Elliptic Curve** by *Valery Asiryan*
statement: EulerBrick.CuboidOne

docstring: The third Cuboid conjecture
statement: EulerBrick.CuboidThree

docstring: Is there an Euler brick in $4$-dimensional space?
statement: True ↔ ∃ sides, EulerBrick.IsEulerHyperBrick 4 sides

docstring: Is there an Euler brick in $n$-dimensional space for any $n > 3$?
statement: True ↔ ∀ n > 3, ∃ sides, EulerBrick.IsEulerHyperBrick n sides

docstring: The second Cuboid conjecture
statement: EulerBrick.CuboidTwo

docstring: Is there a perfect Euler brick?
statement: True ↔ ∃ a b c, EulerBrick.IsPerfectCuboid a b c

docstring:
In [Sh12], Ruslan notes that a perfect Euler brick does not exist
if all three Cuboid conjectures hold.
statement: EulerBrick.CuboidOne → EulerBrick.CuboidTwo → EulerBrick.CuboidThree → ¬∃ a b c, EulerBrick.IsPerfectCuboid a b c

docstring:
**Andrica's conjecture**
The inequality $\sqrt{p_{n+1}}-\sqrt{p_n} < 1$ holds for all $n$, where $p_n$ is the $n$-th prime number.
statement: ∀ (n : ℕ), √↑(Nat.nth Nat.Prime (n + 1)) - √↑(Nat.nth Nat.Prime n) < 1

docstring: Ferreira proved that Andrica's conjecture is true for sufficiently large n.
statement: ∀ᶠ (n : ℕ) in Filter.atTop, √↑(Nat.nth Nat.Prime (n + 1)) - √↑(Nat.nth Nat.Prime n) < 1

docstring:
Does every finite partially ordered set that is not totally ordered
contain two elements $x$ and $y$ such that the probability that
$x$ appears before $y$ in a random linear extension is between $\frac 1 3$ and $\frac 2 3$?

The set of all total order extensions is represented as order preserving
bijections $P$ of $1, ..., n$.
statement:
True ↔
  ∀ (P : Type) [Finite P] [inst : PartialOrder P],
    (¬Std.Total fun x1 x2 => x1 ≤ x2) →
      ∀ (total_ext : Set (P →o ℕ)),
        (∀ (σ : P →o ℕ), σ ∈ total_ext ↔ Set.range ⇑σ = Set.Icc 1 (Nat.card P)) →
          ∃ x y, ↑{σ | σ ∈ total_ext ∧ σ x < σ y}.ncard / ↑total_ext.ncard ∈ Set.Icc (1 / 3) (2 / 3)

docstring: For example, `0` is part of an attracting `2`-cycle of `z ↦ z ^ 2 - 1`.
statement: Mandelbrot.IsAttractingCycle (fun z => z ^ 2 - 1) 2 0

docstring:
The `multibrotSet n` is equivalently the set of all parameters `c` for which the orbit of `0`
under `z ↦ z ^ n + c` does not leave the closed disk of radius `2 ^ (n - 1)⁻¹` around the origin.
statement: ∀ {n : ℕ}, 2 ≤ n → Mandelbrot.multibrotSet n = {c | ∀ (k : ℕ), ‖(fun z => z ^ n + c)^[k] 0‖ ≤ 2 ^ (↑n - 1)⁻¹}

docstring:
On the other hand, while `2` is part of a `1`-cycle of `z ↦ z ^ 2 - 2`, that cycle is not
attracting.
statement: ¬Mandelbrot.IsAttractingCycle (fun z => z ^ 2 - 2) 1 2

docstring: The MLC conjecture, stating that the mandelbrot set is locally connected.
statement: LocallyConnectedSpace ↑Mandelbrot.mandelbrotSet

docstring:
The boundary of any Multibrot set is conjectured to have zero area.
Note that we don't need to exclude the trivial cases `n = 0` and `n = 1` because the conjecture
holds for them.
statement: ∀ {n : ℕ}, MeasureTheory.volume (frontier (Mandelbrot.multibrotSet n)) = 0

docstring:
The boundary of any Multibrot set is measurable because it is closed, so it makes sense to
ask about its area.
statement: ∀ {n : ℕ}, MeasurableSet (frontier (Mandelbrot.multibrotSet n))

docstring: The boundary of the Mandelbrot set is conjectured to have zero area.
statement: MeasureTheory.volume (frontier Mandelbrot.mandelbrotSet) = 0

docstring:
The density of hyperbolicity conjecture for Multibrot sets, stating that the set of all
parameters `c` for which `fun z ↦ z ^ n + c` has an attracting cycle is dense in `multibrotSet n`.
Note that we need to require `2 ≤ n` because the conjecture is trivially false for `n = 1`.
statement:
∀ {n : ℕ},
  2 ≤ n → Mandelbrot.multibrotSet n ⊆ closure {c | ∃ m z, Mandelbrot.IsAttractingCycle (fun z => z ^ n + c) m z}

docstring:
No function has an attracting cycle of period `0`. This is important in that it means we don't
need to require `0 < n` in the conjectures below.
statement: ∀ (f : ℂ → ℂ) (z : ℂ), ¬Mandelbrot.IsAttractingCycle f 0 z

docstring:
The mandelbrot set is equivalently the set of all parameters `c` for which the orbit of `0`
under `z ↦ z ^ 2 + c` does not leave the closed disk of radius two around the origin.
statement: Mandelbrot.mandelbrotSet = {c | ∀ (k : ℕ), ‖(fun z => z ^ 2 + c)^[k] 0‖ ≤ 2}

docstring:
A stronger version of the MLC conjecture, stating that all multibrots are locally connected.
Note that we don't need to require `2 ≤ n` because the conjecture holds in the trivial cases `n = 0`
and `n = 1` too.
statement: ∀ (n : ℕ), LocallyConnectedSpace ↑(Mandelbrot.multibrotSet n)

docstring:
The density of hyperbolicity conjecture, stating that the set of all parameters `c` for which
`fun z ↦ z ^ 2 + c` has an attracting cycle is dense in the Mandelbrot set.
statement: Mandelbrot.mandelbrotSet ⊆ closure {c | ∃ m z, Mandelbrot.IsAttractingCycle (fun z => z ^ 2 + c) m z}

docstring:
It is conjectured that there are infinitely many Wolstenholme primes.

*Reference:* [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolstenholme_prime#Expected_number_of_Wolstenholme_primes)
statement: {p | WolstenholmePrime.IsWolstenholmePrime p}.Infinite
WolstenholmePrime.IsWolstenholmePrime 2124679

docstring:
Wolstenholme's theorem states that any prime $p > 3$ satisfies $\binom{2p-1}{p-1} \equiv 1 (\pmod{p^3})$.

Formal proof linked here provided by AlphaProof.
*Reference:* [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolstenholme%27s_theorem)
statement: ∀ p > 3, Nat.Prime p → (2 * p - 1).choose (p - 1) ≡ 1 [MOD p ^ 3]

docstring:
Two known Wolstenholme primes: 16843 and 2124679.

Formal proof linked here provided by AlphaProof
statement: WolstenholmePrime.IsWolstenholmePrime 16843

docstring: Equivalently, a prime $p > 7$ is a Wolstenholme prime if it divides the numerator of the Bernoulli number $B_{p-3}$.
statement: ∀ (p : ℕ), WolstenholmePrime.IsWolstenholmePrime p ↔ p > 7 ∧ Nat.Prime p ∧ ↑p ∣ (bernoulli' (p - 3)).num

docstring:
Another equivalent definition is that a prime $p > 7$ is a Wolstenholme prime
if it $p^3$ divides the numerator of the harmonic number $H_{p-1}$.
statement: ∀ (p : ℕ), WolstenholmePrime.IsWolstenholmePrime p ↔ p > 7 ∧ Nat.Prime p ∧ ↑(p ^ 3) ∣ (harmonic (p - 1)).num

docstring: Is $\ln(\pi)$ irrational?
statement: True ↔ Irrational (Real.log Real.pi)

docstring: Is the Catalan constant $$G = \sum_{n=0}^∞ (-1)^n / (2n + 1)^2 \approx 0.91596$$ irrational?
statement: True ↔ Irrational catalanConstant

docstring: Is $\pi ^ e$ irrational?
statement: True ↔ Irrational (Real.pi ^ Real.exp 1)

docstring: Is $\pi ^ \pi$ irrational?
statement: True ↔ Irrational (Real.pi ^ Real.pi)

docstring: Is $e + \pi$ irrational?
statement: True ↔ Irrational (Real.exp 1 + Real.pi)

docstring: Is $e ^ e$ irrational?
statement: True ↔ Irrational (Real.exp 1 ^ Real.exp 1)

docstring: Are $e$ and $\pi$ algebraically independent?
statement: True ↔ AlgebraicIndependent ℚ ![Real.exp 1, Real.pi]

docstring: Is $e \pi$ irrational?
statement: True ↔ Irrational (Real.exp 1 * Real.pi)

docstring: Is the Euler-Mascheroni constant $\gamma$ irrational?
statement: True ↔ Irrational Real.eulerMascheroniConstant

docstring:
Can every odd integer greater than 5 be written as the sum of three primes?
(A prime may be used more than once.)

NB. While Harald Helfgott's solution is not published in a peer-reviewed journal yet,
his results seem generally accepted.
statement: ∀ (n : ℕ), 5 < n → Odd n → ∃ p q r, Nat.Prime p ∧ Nat.Prime q ∧ Nat.Prime r ∧ n = p + q + r

docstring: Can every even integer greater than 2 be written as the sum of two primes?
statement: True ↔ ∀ (n : ℕ), 2 < n → Even n → ∃ p q, Prime p ∧ Prime q ∧ n = p + q

docstring: The Noether problem has a positive solution in the three indeterminate case.
statement:
∀ {K L ι : Type} {G : Type} [inst : Field K] [inst_1 : Field L] [inst_2 : Fintype ι] [inst_3 : Algebra K L]
  [inst_4 : NoetherProblem.IsRationalExtension K L ι], Fintype.card ι = 3 → NoetherProblem.HasNoetherProperty K L ι

docstring: The Noether problem has a positive solution in the two indeterminate case.
statement:
∀ {K L ι : Type} {G : Type} [inst : Field K] [inst_1 : Field L] [inst_2 : Fintype ι] [inst_3 : Algebra K L]
  [inst_4 : NoetherProblem.IsRationalExtension K L ι], Fintype.card ι = 2 → NoetherProblem.HasNoetherProperty K L ι

docstring: The Noether problem has a positive solution in the four indeterminate case.
statement:
∀ {K L ι : Type} {G : Type} [inst : Field K] [inst_1 : Field L] [inst_2 : Fintype ι] [inst_3 : Algebra K L]
  [inst_4 : NoetherProblem.IsRationalExtension K L ι], Fintype.card ι = 4 → NoetherProblem.HasNoetherProperty K L ι

docstring:
If the index set `ι` is empty, then `IsRationalExtension K L ι` means that
`K, L` are isomorphic as `K` algebras.
statement:
∀ (K : Type u_1) (L : Type u_2) (ι : Type u_3) [inst : Field K] [inst_1 : Field L] [inst_2 : Algebra K L] [IsEmpty ι]
  [NoetherProblem.IsRationalExtension K L ι], Nonempty (L ≃ₐ[K] K)

docstring:
The **Noether Problem**: let `L` be the field of rational functions in `n`
indeterminates over `K`. Is it true that `L/K` has the Noether property?

Solution: False.
statement:
False ↔
  ∀ (K L ι G : Type) [inst : Field K] [inst_1 : Field L] [inst_2 : Fintype ι] [inst_3 : Algebra K L]
    [inst_4 : NoetherProblem.IsRationalExtension K L ι], NoetherProblem.HasNoetherProperty K L ι

docstring:
One can find a counterexample to the Noether Problem's claim by considering a
rational function field in 47 indeterminates.
statement:
∃ K L ι G x x_1 x_2 x_3,
  ∃ (x_4 : NoetherProblem.IsRationalExtension K L ι), Fintype.card ι = 47 ∧ ¬NoetherProblem.HasNoetherProperty K L ι

docstring:
Let $G$ be a finitely generated group, and assume there exists $n$ such that for every $g$ in $G$,
$g^n = 1$. Is $G$ necessarily finite?
statement: True ↔ ∀ (G : Type) [inst : Group G], Group.FG G → ∀ n > 0, (∀ (g : G), g ^ n = 1) → Finite G

docstring:
**Sendov's conjecture** states that for a polynomial
$$f(z)=(z-r_{1})\cdots (z-r_{n}),\qquad (n\geq 2)$$
with all roots $r_1, ..., r_n$ inside the closed unit disk $|z| ≤ 1$, each of the $n$ roots is at a
distance no more than $1$ from at least one critical point.
statement: ∀ (n : ℕ), 2 ≤ n → Sendov.Nat.SatisfiesSendovConjecture n

docstring:
**Sendov's conjecture** states that for a polynomial
$$f(z)=(z-r_{1})\cdots (z-r_{n}),\qquad (n\geq 2)$$
with all roots $r_1, ..., r_n$ inside the closed unit disk $|z| ≤ 1$, each of the $n$ roots is at a
distance no more than $1$ from at least one critical point.

It has been shown that Sendov's conjecture holds when the degree of $n$ is at most $9$.
statement: ∀ n ∈ Set.Icc 2 9, Sendov.Nat.SatisfiesSendovConjecture n

docstring:
**Sendov's conjecture** states that for a polynomial
$$f(z)=(z-r_{1})\cdots (z-r_{n}),\qquad (n\geq 2)$$
with all roots $r_1, ..., r_n$ inside the closed unit disk $|z| ≤ 1$, each of the $n$ roots is at a
distance no more than $1$ from at least one critical point.

It has been shown that Sendov's conjecture holds for polynomials of sufficiently large degree.
statement: ∀ᶠ (n : ℕ) in Filter.atTop, Sendov.Nat.SatisfiesSendovConjecture n

docstring:
Cyclic groups of perfect number order are Leinster groups.

This follows from the fact that for a cyclic group, all subgroups are normal and correspond
to divisors of the group order, and a number is perfect if and only if the sum of its divisors
(including itself) equals twice the number.
statement:
∀ (G : Type u_1) [inst : Group G] [inst_1 : Fintype G] [IsCyclic G],
  (Fintype.card G).Perfect → LeinsterGroup.IsLeinster G

docstring:
**Conjecture:** Are there infinitely many Leinster groups?

This asks whether there exist infinitely many (non-isomorphic) finite groups that are
Leinster groups.

Formalized via the negation of "Does there exist an n such that all Leinster groups have
order less than n".
statement: True ↔ ¬∃ n, ∀ (G : Type) (x : Group G) (x_1 : Fintype G), LeinsterGroup.IsLeinster G → Fintype.card G < n

docstring:
Non-abelian Leinster groups exist.

For example, `S₃ × C₅` (order 30) and `A₅ × C₁₅₁₂₈` are Leinster groups.

Reference: Leinster, Tom (2001). "Perfect numbers and groups".
statement: ∃ G x x_1, LeinsterGroup.IsLeinster G ∧ ¬∀ (a b : G), a * b = b * a

docstring:
An abelian group is a Leinster group if and only if it is cyclic with order equal
to a perfect number.

Reference: Leinster, Tom (2001). "Perfect numbers and groups". Theorem 2.1.
statement:
∀ (G : Type u_1) [inst : CommGroup G] [inst_1 : Fintype G],
  LeinsterGroup.IsLeinster G ↔ IsCyclic G ∧ (Fintype.card G).Perfect

docstring:
The dihedral group `DihedralGroup n` (of order `2n`) is a Leinster group if and only if `n` is
an odd perfect number. This gives a one-to-one correspondence between dihedral Leinster groups
and odd perfect numbers.

In particular, the existence of odd perfect numbers is equivalent to the existence of
dihedral Leinster groups.

Reference: Leinster, Tom (2001). "Perfect numbers and groups".
statement: ∀ (n : ℕ) [inst : NeZero n], LeinsterGroup.IsLeinster (DihedralGroup n) ↔ n.Perfect ∧ Odd n

docstring:
The Modularity Theorem (formerly Shimura-Taniyama-Weil conjecture): every elliptic curve
over $\mathbb{Q}$ is modular.
statement: ∀ (E : WeierstrassCurve ℚ) [inst : E.IsElliptic], ModularityConjecture.modularityConjecture E

docstring:
Kummer–Vandiver conjecture states that for every prime $p$, the class number of the maximal
real subfield of $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_p)$ is not divisible by $p$.
-
statement: ∀ (p : ℕ+), p.Prime → ¬↑p ∣ NumberField.classNumber ↥(NumberField.maximalRealSubfield (CyclotomicField ↑p ℚ))

docstring: The Cookson Hills series summing $sec(n)^2 / n^3$ from $n=1$ to $\infty$ converges.
statement: True ↔ Summable fun n => 1 / ((↑n + 1) ^ 3 * Real.cos (↑n + 1) ^ 2)

docstring:
The Flint Hills series summing $csc(n)^2 / n^3$ from $n=1$ to $\infty$ converges.
(Note that we 0-index the series below.)
statement: True ↔ Summable fun n => 1 / ((↑n + 1) ^ 3 * Real.sin (↑n + 1) ^ 2)

docstring:
If there exists a constant `c > 0` such that
`(n + 1).nth Nat.Prime - n.nth Nat.Prime < (n.nth Nat.Prime) ^ (1 / 2 - c)` for all large `n`,
then Legendre's conjecture is asymptotically true.

Formal proof linked here provided by AlphaProof.
statement:
(∃ c > 0,
    ∀ᶠ (n : ℕ) in Filter.atTop,
      ↑(Nat.nth Nat.Prime (n + 1)) - ↑(Nat.nth Nat.Prime n) < ↑(Nat.nth Nat.Prime n) ^ (1 / 2 - c)) →
  ∀ᶠ (n : ℕ) in Filter.atTop, ∃ p ∈ Set.Ioo (n ^ 2) ((n + 1) ^ 2), Nat.Prime p

docstring: Ferreira proved that the conjecture is true for sufficiently large n.
statement: ∀ᶠ (n : ℕ) in Filter.atTop, ∃ p ∈ Set.Ioo (n ^ 2) ((n + 1) ^ 2), Nat.Prime p

docstring: Does there always exist at least one prime between consecutive perfect squares?
statement: True ↔ ∀ n ≥ 1, ∃ p ∈ Set.Ioo (n ^ 2) ((n + 1) ^ 2), Nat.Prime p

docstring: Euler's sum of powers conjecture is false for $k=4$ (counterexample exists).
Euler's sum of powers conjecture is false for $k=5$ (counterexample exists).

Euler's sum of powers conjecture states that for integers $n > 1$ and $k > 1$,
if the sum of $n$ positive integers each raised to the $k$-th power equals another integer
raised to the $k$-th power, then $n ≥ k$.

The conjecture is known to be false for $k = 4$ and $k = 5$,
but remains open for $k ≥ 6$.
statement: ∀ (n k b : ℕ), 1 < n → 5 < k → ∀ (a : Fin n → ℕ), (∀ (i : Fin n), a i > 0) → ∑ i, a i ^ k = b ^ k → k ≤ n

docstring:
**Grimm's Conjecture**
If $n, n+1, \dots, n+k-1$ are all composite numbers, then there are $k$ distinct primes $p_i$
such that $p_i$ divides $n + i$ for all $0 \le i \le k-1$.
statement: ∀ (n k : ℕ), 1 ≤ n → 1 ≤ k → (∀ (i : Fin k), (n + ↑i).Composite) → ∃ ps, ∀ (i : Fin k), Nat.Prime (ps i) ∧ ps i ∣ n + ↑i

docstring:
**Grimm's Conjecture, weaker version**
If $n, n+1, \dots, n+k-1$ are all composite numbers, then their product
has at least $k$ distinct prime divisors.
statement:
∀ (n k : ℕ),
  1 ≤ n → 1 ≤ k → (∀ (i : Fin k), (n + ↑i).Composite) → ∃ ps, ∀ (i : Fin k), Nat.Prime (ps i) ∧ ∃ j, ps i ∣ n + ↑j

docstring: Idoneal numbers completeness conjecture.
statement: True ↔ ∀ (n : ℕ), Idoneal.IsIdoneal n → n ∈ Idoneal.knownIdonealNumbers

docstring: All 65 known idoneal numbers are indeed idoneal.
statement: ∀ n ∈ Idoneal.knownIdonealNumbers, Idoneal.IsIdoneal n

docstring:
Singmaster's conjecture: the number of times any number $t > 1$ appears in
Pascal's triangle is bounded.
statement: ∃ C, ∀ t > 1, (Singmaster.solutions t).Finite ∧ (Singmaster.solutions t).ncard ≤ C

docstring:
An upper bound of the maximal length of the longest snake in a box is given by
$$
1 + 2^{n-1}\frac{6n}{6n + \frac{1}{6\sqrt{6}}n^{\frac 1 2} - 7}.
$$
statement: ∀ (n : ℕ), ↑(SnakeInBox.LongestSnakeInTheBox n) ≤ 1 + 2 ^ (n - 1) * (6 * ↑n) / (6 * ↑n + 1 / (6 * √6) * √↑n)

docstring:
The longest snake in the $0$-dimensional cube, i.e. the cube consisting of one point, is zero,
since there only is one induced path and it is of length zero.
statement: SnakeInBox.LongestSnakeInTheBox 0 = 0

docstring: The best length found so far for dimension nine is 190.
statement: 190 ≤ SnakeInBox.LongestSnakeInTheBox 9

docstring:
The maximum length for the snake-in-the-box problem is known for dimensions zero through eight;
it is $0, 1, 2, 4, 7, 13, 26, 50, 98$.
statement: List.map SnakeInBox.LongestSnakeInTheBox (List.range 9) = [0, 1, 2, 4, 7, 13, 26, 50, 98]

docstring:
For dimension $9$, the length of the longest snake in the box is not known.
This is currently the smallest dimension where this question is open.
statement: SnakeInBox.LongestSnakeInTheBox 9 = sorry

docstring: The New Mersenne Conjecture statement holds for odd primes.
statement: ∀ (p : ℕ), Nat.Prime p → Odd p → Mersenne.NewMersenneConjectureStatement p

docstring: It suffices to check this conjecture for primes
statement:
(∀ (p : ℕ), Nat.Prime p → Mersenne.NewMersenneConjectureStatement p) →
  ∀ (p : ℕ), Odd p → Mersenne.NewMersenneConjectureStatement p

docstring:
For any odd natural number `p` if two of the following conditions hold,
then all three must hold:
1. $2^p-1$ is prime
2. $(2^p+1)/3$ is prime
3. Exists a number `k` such that $p = 2^k \\pm 1$ or $p = 4^k \\pm 3$
statement: ∀ (p : ℕ), Odd p → Mersenne.NewMersenneConjectureStatement p

docstring: Are there infinitely many Mersenne primes?
statement: True ↔ {p | Mersenne.Nat.GivesMersennePrime p}.Infinite

docstring: The **Agoh-Giuga Conjecture**, Agoh's formulation
statement: AgohGiuga.AgohGiugaCongr

docstring:
A composite number $n$ is weak Giuga if and only if
$$
\sum_{p\mid n} \frac{1}{p} - \frac{1}{n} \in\mathbb{N}.
$$
statement: ∀ {n : ℕ}, n.Composite → (AgohGiuga.IsWeakGiuga n ↔ ∃ m, ∑ p ∈ n.primeFactors, 1 / ↑p - 1 / ↑n = ↑m)

docstring:
A composite number $n$ is weak Giuga if and only if $p \mid (\frac{n}{p} - 1)$ for all
prime divisors $p$ of $n$.
statement: ∀ {n : ℕ}, n.Composite → (AgohGiuga.IsWeakGiuga n ↔ ∀ p ∈ n.primeFactors, p ∣ n / p - 1)

docstring:
Giuga showed that a Giuga number has at least 9 prime factors.
Ref: G. Giuga, _Su una presumibile proprieta caratteristica dei numeri primi_
statement: ∀ (a : ℕ), AgohGiuga.IsStrongGiuga a → 9 ≤ a.primeFactors.card

docstring: The two statements of the conjecture are equivalent.
statement: AgohGiuga.AgohGiugaCongr ↔ AgohGiuga.AgohGiugaSum

docstring: The **Agoh-Giuga Conjecture**, Giuga's formulation
statement: AgohGiuga.AgohGiugaSum

docstring:
A composite number `a` is Carmichael if and only if it is squarefree
and, for all prime `p` dividing `a`, we have `p - 1 ∣ a - 1`.
statement: ∀ (a : ℕ), a.Composite → (AgohGiuga.IsCarmichael a ↔ Squarefree a ∧ ∀ (p : ℕ), Nat.Prime p → p ∣ a → p - 1 ∣ a - 1)

docstring:
Giuga showed that a number `n` is strong Giuga if and only if it is
Carmichael and `∑_{p|n} 1/p - 1/n ∈ ℕ` (i.e., if and only if it is Carmichael
and weak Giuga).
Ref: G. Giuga, _Su una presumibile proprieta caratteristica dei numeri primi_
statement:
∀ {a : ℕ},
  a.Composite → (AgohGiuga.IsStrongGiuga a ↔ AgohGiuga.IsCarmichael a ∧ ∃ n, ∑ p ∈ a.primeFactors, 1 / ↑p - 1 / ↑a = ↑n)

docstring:
Let `G(X)` denote the number of exceptions `n ≤ X` to Giuga’s conjecture.
Then for `X` larger than an absolute constant which can be made
explicit, `G(X) ≪ X^{1/2} log X`.
Ref: Vicentiu Tipu, _A Note on Giuga’s Conjecture_
statement:
∀ (G : ℕ → ℕ),
  (G = fun x => (Finset.filter AgohGiuga.IsStrongGiuga (Finset.Icc 1 x)).card) →
    ∃ N O, ∀ n ≥ N, ↑(G n) ≤ O * √↑n * Real.log ↑n

docstring: A composite Carmichael number is squarefree.
statement: ∀ {a : ℕ}, a.Composite → AgohGiuga.IsCarmichael a → Squarefree a

docstring: Every strong Giuga number is a Carmichael number.
statement: ∀ (a : ℕ), AgohGiuga.IsStrongGiuga a → AgohGiuga.IsCarmichael a

docstring:
There is a convex set of area 0.270911861 that covers all worms.

*Reference:*
Wang, Wei (2006), "An improved upper bound for the worm problem",
Acta Mathematica Sinica, 49 (4): 835–846, MR 2264090.
statement:
∃ X,
  MeasurableSet X ∧
    Convex ℝ X ∧
      MeasureTheory.volume X = 0.270911861 ∧
        ∀ w ∈ MoserWorm.Worms, ∃ e v, LinearEquiv.det e.toLinearEquiv = 1 ∧ w ⊆ (fun x => e x + v) '' X

docstring:
There is a set of area 0.260437 that covers all worms.

*Reference:*
Norwood, Rick; Poole, George (2003), "An improved upper bound for Leo Moser's worm problem",
Discrete and Computational Geometry, 29 (3): 409–417, doi:10.1007/s00454-002-0774-3, MR 1961007.
statement: ∃ X ∈ MoserWorm.WormCovers, MeasureTheory.volume X = 0.260437

docstring:
**Convex Moser's Worm Problem**
What is the minimal area (or greatest lower bound on the area)
of a *convex* shape that can cover every unit-length curve?
statement: IsGLB {v | ∃ X ∈ MoserWorm.WormCovers, Convex ℝ X ∧ MeasureTheory.volume X = v} sorry

docstring:
A disc of radius 1 / 2 is a worm cover.

This follows by translating the center of the disc to the midpoint of the worm.
statement: Metric.closedBall 0 0.5 ∈ MoserWorm.WormCovers

docstring:
**Moser's Worm Problem**
What is the minimal area (or greatest lower bound on the area)
of a shape that can cover every unit-length curve?
statement: IsGLB {v | ∃ X ∈ MoserWorm.WormCovers, MeasureTheory.volume X = v} sorry

docstring:
0.232239 is a lower bound on the area of a convex set that covers all worms.

*Reference:*
Khandhawit, Tirasan; Pagonakis, Dimitrios; Sriswasdi, Sira (2013),
"Lower Bound for Convex Hull Area and Universal Cover Problems",
International Journal of Computational Geometry & Applications,
23 (3): 197–212, arXiv:1101.5638, doi:10.1142/S0218195913500076, MR 3158583, S2CID 207132316.
statement: 0.232239 ∈ lowerBounds {v | ∃ X ∈ MoserWorm.WormCovers, Convex ℝ X ∧ MeasureTheory.volume X = v}

docstring:
The minimal area of a convex shape that can cover every unit-length curve is attained.
This follows from the Blaschke selection theorem.
statement: ∃ bound, IsLeast {v | ∃ X ∈ MoserWorm.WormCovers, Convex ℝ X ∧ MeasureTheory.volume X = v} bound

docstring: The only clique of size `n` in a complete graph on `n` vertices is the entire set of vertices.
statement: ∀ {V : Type} [inst : Fintype V], ⊤.cliqueSet (Fintype.card V) = {Set.univ.toFinset}
Conway99Graph.Conway9.LocallyLinear

docstring: The triangle is an example with 3 vertices satisfying the condition.
statement:
(SimpleGraph.completeGraph (Fin 3)).LocallyLinear ∧
  Conway99Graph.NonEdgesAreDiagonals (SimpleGraph.completeGraph (Fin 3))

docstring:
Does there exist an undirected graph with 99 vertices, in which each two adjacent vertices have
exactly one common neighbor, and in which each two non-adjacent vertices have exactly two common
neighbors?
Equivalently, every edge should be part of a unique triangle and every non-adjacent pair should be
one of the two diagonals of a unique 4-cycle.
The first condition is equivalent to being locally linear.
statement: True ↔ ∃ G, G.LocallyLinear ∧ Conway99Graph.NonEdgesAreDiagonals G
Conway99Graph.NonEdgesAreDiagonals Conway99Graph.Conway9

docstring: A finset of vertices in a complete graph is always a clique.
statement: ∀ {V : Type} (s : Finset V), ⊤.IsClique ↑s

(SimpleGraph.completeGraph (Fin 3) □ SimpleGraph.completeGraph (Fin 3)).cliqueSet 3 =
  {x | ∃ q, {x | ∃ p, (p, q) = x} = x} ∪ {x | ∃ q, {x | ∃ p, (q, p) = x} = x}

docstring: Oppermann's conjecture implies Brocard's conjecture.
statement:
∀ (n : ℕ),
  1 ≤ n →
    (∀ (x : ℕ),
        2 ≤ x →
          (∃ p ∈ Finset.Ioo (x * (x - 1)) (x ^ 2), Nat.Prime p) ∧ ∃ p ∈ Finset.Ioo (x ^ 2) (x * (x + 1)), Nat.Prime p) →
      4 ≤ (Finset.filter Nat.Prime (Finset.Ioo (Nat.nth Nat.Prime n ^ 2) (Nat.nth Nat.Prime (n + 1) ^ 2))).card

docstring: For every integer $x \ge 2$ there exists a prime between $x(x-1)$ and $x^2$.
statement: ∀ (x : ℕ), 2 ≤ x → ∃ p ∈ Finset.Ioo (x * (x - 1)) (x ^ 2), Nat.Prime p

docstring: Oppermann's conjecture implies Legendre's conjecture.
statement:
∀ (n : ℕ),
  1 ≤ n →
    (∀ (x : ℕ),
        2 ≤ x →
          (∃ p ∈ Finset.Ioo (x * (x - 1)) (x ^ 2), Nat.Prime p) ∧ ∃ p ∈ Finset.Ioo (x ^ 2) (x * (x + 1)), Nat.Prime p) →
      ∃ p ∈ Finset.Ioo (n ^ 2) ((n + 1) ^ 2), Nat.Prime p

docstring:
**Oppermann's Conjecture**:
For every integer $x \ge 2$, the following hold:
- There exists a prime between $x(x-1)$ and $x^2$.
- There exists a prime between $x^2$ and $x(x+1)$.
statement:
∀ (x : ℕ),
  2 ≤ x → (∃ p ∈ Finset.Ioo (x * (x - 1)) (x ^ 2), Nat.Prime p) ∧ ∃ p ∈ Finset.Ioo (x ^ 2) (x * (x + 1)), Nat.Prime p

docstring: For every integer $x \ge 2$ there exists a prime between $x^2$ and $x(x+1)$.
statement: ∀ (x : ℕ), 2 ≤ x → ∃ p ∈ Finset.Ioo (x ^ 2) (x * (x + 1)), Nat.Prime p

docstring: Ferreira proved that Oppermann's conjecture is true for sufficiently large x.
statement:
∀ᶠ (x : ℕ) in Filter.atTop,
  (∃ p ∈ Finset.Ioo (x * (x - 1)) (x ^ 2), Nat.Prime p) ∧ ∃ p ∈ Finset.Ioo (x ^ 2) (x * (x + 1)), Nat.Prime p

docstring:
**Quasiperfect Numbers Conjecture.**
Do quasiperfect numbers exist?
statement: True ↔ ∃ n, QuasiperfectNumbers.Quasiperfect n

docstring:
**Inscribed square problem**
Does every Jordan curve admit an inscribed square?
statement:
True ↔

docstring:
**The Bateman-Horn Conjecture**
Given a finite collection of distinct irreducible polynomials non-constant $f_1, f_2, \dots, f_k \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$
with positive leading coefficients that satisfy the Schinzel condition, the number
of positive integers n ≤ x for which all polynomials $f_i$ are simultaneously prime is asymptotic to:
$$C(f_1, f_2, \dots, f_k) x / (log x)^k$$
where $C$ is the Bateman-Horn constant given by the convergent infinite product:
$$C = \frac{1}{D}\prod_{p\in\mathbb{P}} (1 - 1/p)^(-k) · (1 - \omega_p/p)$$
Here $\omega_p/p$ is the number of residue classes modulo $p$ for which at least one polynomial vanishes.

The Schinzel condition ensures that for each prime $p$, there exists some integer $n$
such that $p$ does not divide the product $f_(n) f_2(n) \dotsb f_(n)$, which guarantees the
infinite product converges to a positive value.
statement:
∀ (polys : Finset (Polynomial ℤ)),
  polys.Nonempty →
    (∀ f ∈ polys, BunyakovskyCondition f) →
      SchinzelCondition polys →
        Asymptotics.IsEquivalent Filter.atTop (fun x => ↑(BatemanHornConjecture.CountSimultaneousPrimes polys x))
          fun x => BatemanHornConjecture.BatemanHornConstant polys * x / Real.log x ^ polys.card

docstring:
[BMO#5](https://wiki.bbchallenge.org/wiki/Beaver_Math_Olympiad#5._1RB0LD_1LC0RA_1RA1LB_1LA1LE_1RF0LC_---0RE_(bbch))

Let $(a_n)_{n \ge 1}$ and $(b_n)_{n \ge 1}$ be two sequences such that $(a_1, b_1) = (0, 5)$ and

$$(a_{n+1}, b_{n+1}) = \begin{cases}
(a_n+1, b_n-f(a_n)) & \text{if } b_n \ge f(a_n) \\
(a_n, 3b_n+a_n+5) & \text{if } b_n < f(a_n)
\end{cases}$$

where $f(x)=10\cdot 2^x-1$ for all non-negative integers $x$.

Does there exist a positive integer $i$ such that $b_i = f(a_i)-1$?

[BMO#5](https://wiki.bbchallenge.org/wiki/Beaver_Math_Olympiad#5._1RB0LD_1LC0RA_1RA1LB_1LA1LE_1RF0LC_---0RE_(bbch)) is equivalent to asking whether the 6-state Turing machine
[`1RB0LD_1LC0RA_1RA1LB_1LA1LE_1RF0LC_---0RE`](https://wiki.bbchallenge.org/wiki/1RB0LD_1LC0RA_1RA1LB_1LA1LE_1RF0LC_---0RE) halts or not.

There is presently no consensus on whether the machine halts or not, hence the problem is formulated
using `answer(sorry) ↔`.

The machine was discovered by [bbchallenge.org](bbchallenge.org) contributor mxdys
on August 7th 2024.

The correspondence between the machine's halting problem and the below reformulation has been proven
in [Rocq](https://github.com/ccz181078/busycoq/blob/BB6/verify/1RB0LD_1LC0RA_1RA1LB_1LA1LE_1RF0LC_---0RE.v).
statement:
True ↔
  ∀ (a b f : ℕ → ℕ),
    (f = fun x => 10 * 2 ^ x - 1) →
      a 0 = 0 →
        b 0 = 5 →
          (∀ (n : ℕ), a (n + 1) = if f (a n) ≤ b n then a n + 1 else a n) →
            (∀ (n : ℕ), b (n + 1) = if f (a n) ≤ b n then b n - f (a n) else 3 * b n + a n + 5) → ∃ i, b i = f (a i) - 1

docstring:
[BMO#3][https://wiki.bbchallenge.org/wiki/Beaver_Math_Olympiad#3._1RB0RB3LA4LA2RA_2LB3RA---3RA4RB_(bbch)_and_1RB1RB3LA4LA2RA_2LB3RA---3RA4RB_(bbch)]

Let $v_2(n)$ be the largest integer $k$ such that $2^k$ divides $n$.
Let $(a_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be a sequence such that

$$a_n = \begin{cases}
2 & \text{if } n=0 \\
a_{n-1}+2^{v_2(a_{n-1})+2}-1 & \text{if } n \ge 1
\end{cases}$$

for all non-negative integers $n$. Is there an integer $n$ such that $a_n=4^k$ for
some positive integer $k$?

[BMO#3][https://wiki.bbchallenge.org/wiki/Beaver_Math_Olympiad#3._1RB0RB3LA4LA2RA_2LB3RA---3RA4RB_(bbch)_and_1RB1RB3LA4LA2RA_2LB3RA---3RA4RB_(bbch)] is equivalent to the non-termination of 2-state 5-symbol Turing machine [`1RB0RB3LA4LA2RA_2LB3RA---3RA4RB`](https://wiki.bbchallenge.org/wiki/1RB0RB3LA4LA2RA_2LB3RA---3RA4RB) (from all-0 tape).

The machine was found and informally proven not to halt by [bbchallenge.org](bbchallenge.org)
contributor Daniel Yuan on June 18th 2024; see [Discord discussion](https://discord.com/channels/960643023006490684/1084047886494470185/1252634913220591728).
statement: ∀ (a : ℕ → ℕ), a 0 = 2 → (∀ (n : ℕ), a (n + 1) = a n + 2 ^ (padicValNat 2 (a n) + 2) - 1) → ¬∃ n k, a n = 4 ^ k

docstring:
[BMO#1](https://wiki.bbchallenge.org/wiki/Beaver_Math_Olympiad#1._1RB1RE_1LC0RA_0RD1LB_---1RC_1LF1RE_0LB0LE_(bbch))

Let $(a_n)_{n \ge 1}$ and $(b_n)_{n \ge 1}$ be two sequences such that $(a_1, b_1) = (1, 2)$ and

$$(a_{n+1}, b_{n+1}) = \begin{cases}
(a_n-b_n, 4b_n+2) & \text{if }a_n \ge b_n \\
(2a_n+1, b_n-a_n) & \text{if }a_n < b_n
\end{cases}$$

for all positive integers $n$. Does there exist a positive integer $i$ such that $a_i = b_i$?

The first 10 values of $(a_n, b_n)$ are $(1, 2), (3, 1), (2, 6), (5, 4), (1, 18), (3, 17),
(7, 14), (15, 7), (8, 30), (17, 22)$.

[BMO#1](https://wiki.bbchallenge.org/wiki/Beaver_Math_Olympiad#1._1RB1RE_1LC0RA_0RD1LB_---1RC_1LF1RE_0LB0LE_(bbch)) is equivalent to asking whether the 6-state Turing machine
[`1RB1RE_1LC0RA_0RD1LB_---1RC_1LF1RE_0LB0LE`](https://wiki.bbchallenge.org/wiki/1RB1RE_1LC0RA_0RD1LB_---1RC_1LF1RE_0LB0LE) halts or not.

There is presently no consensus on whether the machine halts or not, hence the problem is formulated
using `answer(sorry) ↔`.

The machine was discovered by [bbchallenge.org](bbchallenge.org) contributor Jason Yuen on
June 25th 2024.
statement:
True ↔
  ∀ (a b : ℕ → ℕ),
    a 0 = 1 →
      (∀ (n : ℕ), a (n + 1) = if b n ≤ a n then a n - b n else 2 * a n + 1) →
        b 0 = 2 → (∀ (n : ℕ), b (n + 1) = if b n ≤ a n then 4 * b n + 2 else b n - a n) → ∃ i, a i = b i

docstring:
[BMO#2](https://wiki.bbchallenge.org/wiki/Beaver_Math_Olympiad#2._Hydra_and_Antihydra)

Antihydra is a sequence starting at 8, and iterating the function
$$H(n) = \left\lfloor \frac {3n}2 \right\rfloor.$$
The conjecture states that the cumulative number of odd values in this sequence
is never more than twice the cumulative number of even values. It is a relatively new open problem
with, so it might be solvable, although seems quite hard because of its Collatz-like flavor.
The underlying Collatz-like map has been studied independently in the past,
see doi:[10.1017/S0017089508004655](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0017089508004655) (Corollary 4).

It is equivalent to non-termination of the [`1RB1RA_0LC1LE_1LD1LC_1LA0LB_1LF1RE_---0RA`](https://wiki.bbchallenge.org/wiki/Antihydra) 6-state Turing machine (from all-0 tape). Note that the conjecture
that the machine does not halt is based on [a probabilistic argument](https://wiki.bbchallenge.org/wiki/Antihydra#Trajectory).

This machine and its mathematical reformulations were found by [bbchallenge.org](bbchallenge.org)
contributors mxdys and Rachel Hunter on June 28th 2024.

[BMO#4](https://wiki.bbchallenge.org/wiki/Beaver_Math_Olympiad#4._1RB3RB---1LB0LA_2LA4RA3LA4RB1LB_(bbch))

Bonnie the beaver was bored, so she tried to construct a sequence of integers $\{a_n\}_{n \ge 0}$.
She first defined $a_0=2$, then defined $a_{n+1}$ depending on $a_n$ and $n$
using the following rules:

* If $a_n \equiv 0\text{ (mod 3)}$, then $a_{n+1}=\frac{a_n}{3}+2^n+1$.
* If $a_n \equiv 2\text{ (mod 3)}$, then $a_{n+1}=\frac{a_n-2}{3}+2^n-1$.

With these two rules alone, Bonnie calculates the first few terms in the sequence: $2, 0, 3, 6, 11,
18, 39, 78, 155, 306, \dots$. At this point, Bonnie plans to continue writing terms until a term
becomes $1\text{ (mod 3)}$. If Bonnie sticks to her plan, will she ever finish?

[BMO#4](https://wiki.bbchallenge.org/wiki/Beaver_Math_Olympiad#4._1RB3RB---1LB0LA_2LA4RA3LA4RB1LB_(bbch))
is equivalent to the non-termination of 2-state 5-symbol Turing machine
[`1RB3RB---1LB0LA_2LA4RA3LA4RB1LB`](https://wiki.bbchallenge.org/wiki/1RB3RB---1LB0LA_2LA4RA3LA4RB1LB) (from all-0 tape).

The machine was informally proven not to halt [bbchallenge.org](bbchallenge.org)
contributor Daniel Yuan on July 19th 2024; see [sketched proof](https://wiki.bbchallenge.org/wiki/1RB3RB---1LB0LA_2LA4RA3LA4RB1LB) and [Discord discussion](https://discord.com/channels/960643023006490684/960643023530762343/1263666591900631210).

$$
  \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{\left(\frac{2}{3} + \frac{1}{3}\sin n\right)^n}{n}

converge?

https://github.com/AxiomMath/gdm-formal-conjectures/blob/main/docs/BorweinSineSeries.md
for a partial formalization of the conjecture,
conditional on such an irrationality measure of pi (cf https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.06345).

docstring:
The **Riemann Hypothesis**: all non-trivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function have real
part $\frac{1}{2}$. That is, if $\zeta(s) = 0$, $s \neq 1$, and $s$ is not a trivial zero
$-2(n+1)$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$, then $\operatorname{Re}(s) = \frac{1}{2}$.

This is the official Millennium Prize Problem as posed by the
[Clay Mathematics Institute](https://www.claymath.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/05/riemann.pdf).

This uses the `RiemannHypothesis` type from Mathlib, which is defined as
`∀ (s : ℂ), riemannZeta s = 0 → (¬∃ n : ℕ, s = -2 * (n + 1)) → s ≠ 1 → s.re = 1 / 2`.

Empirical evidence seems to suggest that Slud's bound does not hold for all $p$, and in fact, as $n\to\infty$,
the maximal permissible $p$ shrinks to $\frac{1}{2}$. Also, the following appears to be true:

When $p\in(0,1/2)$ and
$m = 2k$ is even, and $\sigma := \sqrt{p(1-p)}$,
$$
  \mathbb{P}[B(p,m) \geq m/2] \geq 1 - \Phi\left(\frac{(1/2-p)\sqrt{m}}{\sigma}\right) + \frac 1 2\binom{m}{m/2}\sigma^{m}.
$$

A solution of this statement has been put out by Logical Intelligence
https://github.com/logical-intelligence/proofs, see
[here](https://github.com/logical-intelligence/proofs/blob/main/LI/Conj63_informal_proof.md) for
and informal sketch of the proof.
statement:
∀ (p : ℝ) (h_p : p ∈ Set.Ioo 0 (1 / 2)) (k : ℕ) (hk : 0 < k) (σ : ℝ),
  σ = √(p * (1 - p)) →
    1 - ↑(ProbabilityTheory.cdf (ProbabilityTheory.gaussianReal 0 1)) ((1 / 2 - p) * ↑(NNReal.sqrt (2 * ↑k)) / σ) +
        1 / 2 * ↑((2 * k).choose k) * σ ^ (2 * k) ≤
      ((PMF.binomial ⟨p, ⋯⟩ ⋯ (2 * k)).toMeasure (Set.Ici ⟨k, ⋯⟩)).toReal

docstring:
Green's Open Problem 28 is the probabilistic reformulation of Mathoverflow 339137.

Suppose that $X, Y$ are two finitely-supported independent random variables taking integer values,
and such that $X + Y$ is uniformly distributed on its range. Are $X$ and $Y$ themselves uniformly
distributed on their ranges?

Mathematically, this equivalence is established via Probability Generating Functions (PGFs),
shifting the support to $\mathbb{N}$, and appropriately scaling the coefficients.
statement:
(∀ (P Q R : Polynomial ℝ),
    P.Monic →
      Q.Monic →
        (∀ c ∈ P.coeffs, 0 ≤ c) →
          (∀ c ∈ Q.coeffs, 0 ≤ c) →
            R = P * Q →
              Mathoverflow339137.IsZeroOne R → Mathoverflow339137.IsZeroOne P ∧ Mathoverflow339137.IsZeroOne Q) ↔
  (True ↔
    ∀ (X Y : PMF ℤ),
      X.support.Finite ∧ Y.support.Finite ∧ Green28.IsUniformOnSupport (Green28.indepSum X Y) →
        Green28.IsUniformOnSupport X ∧ Green28.IsUniformOnSupport Y)

Does the 6-sphere admit a complex structure, i.e. an atlas of holomorphically compatible charts
relating it to `EuclideanSpace ℂ (Fin 3)`?
statement: True ↔ ∃ atlas, IsManifold (modelWithCornersSelf ℂ (EuclideanSpace ℂ (Fin 3))) 1 ↑(Mathoverflow1973.unitSphere 6)

docstring:
Weaker version proven by Kahn–Kalai: the same conclusion holds when $1000 \log n$ is replaced by
$C_\varepsilon \, n^\varepsilon$ for every fixed $\varepsilon > 0$.
statement:
∀ ε > 0,
  ∃ C > 0,
    ∀ (n : ℕ),
      2 ≤ n →
        ∀ (F : Finset (Finset (Fin n))),
          Mathoverflow10799.IsMonotoneIncreasing F →
            ∀ (s t : ℝ),
              0 < s → s ≤ t → t < 1 → t / s > C * ↑n ^ ε → ∃ p, s ≤ p ∧ p ≤ t ∧ Mathoverflow10799.IsOptimal p F

docstring: The boundary count is zero for the full family (every set is in $\mathcal F$).
statement: ∀ (n : ℕ) (S : Finset (Fin n)), Mathoverflow10799.boundaryCount n Finset.univ S = 0

docstring:
Problem: For every monotone increasing family $F$, given an interval $[s,t]$ of real numbers so
that $t/s > 1000 \log n$ we have some $p$ in the interval $[s,t]$ so that $F$ is optimal with
respect to $\mu_p$.

This was a "missing lemma" in the work of Kahn and Kalai on threshold behavior of monotone
properties. The related [Kahn–Kalai conjecture](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0603218) was
[settled by Park and Pham](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.17207).

**This conjecture is false** without the additional assumption $\mu_t(F) = 1/2$.
A counterexample was found by Shlomo Perles (April 7, 2026).
statement:
False ↔
  ∀ (n : ℕ),
    2 ≤ n →
      ∀ (F : Finset (Finset (Fin n))),
        Mathoverflow10799.IsMonotoneIncreasing F →
          ∀ (s t : ℝ),
            0 < s → s ≤ t → t < 1 → t / s > 1000 * Real.log ↑n → ∃ p, s ≤ p ∧ p ≤ t ∧ Mathoverflow10799.IsOptimal p F

docstring: The edge boundary is zero for the empty family.
statement: ∀ (n : ℕ) (p : ℝ), Mathoverflow10799.edgeBoundary n p ∅ = 0

docstring: The edge boundary is zero for the full family.
statement: ∀ (n : ℕ) (p : ℝ), Mathoverflow10799.edgeBoundary n p Finset.univ = 0

docstring: The boundary count is zero for the empty family (no set is in $\mathcal F$).
statement: ∀ (n : ℕ) (S : Finset (Fin n)), Mathoverflow10799.boundaryCount n ∅ S = 0

docstring:
For $p = 1/2$, the $p$-biased measure is the uniform distribution:
$\mu_{1/2}(S) = (1/2)^n$ for every $S \subseteq [n]$.
statement: ∀ {n : ℕ} (S : Finset (Fin n)), Mathoverflow10799.μ (1 / 2) S = (1 / 2) ^ n

docstring: The measure of the full power set is $1$.
statement: ∀ (n : ℕ) (p : ℝ), Mathoverflow10799.μFamily p Finset.univ = 1

docstring:
The $p$-biased measure is a probability distribution: it sums to $1$ over all subsets.
This is the binomial identity $(p + (1-p))^n = 1$.
statement: ∀ (n : ℕ) (p : ℝ), ∑ S, Mathoverflow10799.μ p S = 1

docstring:
Now a famous isoperimetric relation asserts that
(IR) $I^p(F) \ge \frac{1}{p} \mu_p(F) \log_p \mu_p(F)$
This relation is true for every family $F$ and every $p$. It is especially famous and simple when
$p=1/2$ and $\mu_p(F)=1/2$. In this case, it says that given a set of half the vertices of the
discrete cube $2^X$, the number of edges between $F$ and its complement is at least $2^{n-1}$.

*Note on translation:* We use `Real.logb p m` to represent the logarithm base $p$ directly.
The factor of $p$ in the denominator (equivalent to $1/p$ in front) is consistent with the
definition of `IsOptimal` used in the counterexample proof.
statement:
∀ (n : ℕ) (p : ℝ),
  0 < p →
    p < 1 →
      ∀ (F : Finset (Finset (Fin n))),
        have m := Mathoverflow10799.μFamily p F;
        Mathoverflow10799.edgeBoundary n p F ≥ m * Real.logb p m / p

docstring:
Conjecture 7 from Kahn–Kalai 2006: the same statement as the original
conjecture, but with the additional assumption that $t$ is the critical probability for $F$,
namely $\mu_t(F) = 1/2$.
statement:
True ↔
  ∀ (n : ℕ),
    2 ≤ n →
      ∀ (F : Finset (Finset (Fin n))),
        Mathoverflow10799.IsMonotoneIncreasing F →
          ∀ (s t : ℝ),
            0 < s →
              s ≤ t →
                t < 1 →
                  Mathoverflow10799.μFamily t F = 1 / 2 →
                    t / s > 1000 * Real.log ↑n → ∃ p, s ≤ p ∧ p ≤ t ∧ Mathoverflow10799.IsOptimal p F

docstring:
Test lemma showing that `boundaryCount` is equivalent to counting subsets $T$
that differ from $S$ in exactly one element and exactly one of $S, T$ belongs to $F$.
statement:
∀ (n : ℕ) (F : Finset (Finset (Fin n))) (S : Finset (Fin n)),
  Mathoverflow10799.boundaryCount n F S = {T | (symmDiff S T).card = 1 ∧ Xor' (S ∈ F) (T ∈ F)}.card

docstring:
Is it true that for all `c ≥ 0`, the density `f c` of integers for which
`(p (n + 1) - p n) / log n < c` exists and is a continuous function of `c`?
statement: True ↔ ∃ f, Continuous f ∧ ∀ (c : NNReal), {n | ↑(primeGap n) / Real.log ↑n < ↑c}.HasDensity (f c)

docstring:
Let $P(n)$ denote the largest prime factor of $n$. Show that the set of $n$
with $P(n+1) > P(n)$ has density $\frac{1}{2}$.
statement: {n | (n + 1).maxPrimeFac > n.maxPrimeFac}.HasDensity (1 / 2)

docstring:
Let $A\subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be a set of $n$ points with no three on a line.
Does $A$ determine at least $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ distinct distances?
statement:
True ↔
  ∀ (A : Finset (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 2))),
    EuclideanGeometry.NonTrilinear ↑A → A.card / 2 ≤ EuclideanGeometry.distinctDistances A

docstring:
Let $A\subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be a set of $n$ points with no three on a line.
Must there exist a single point from which there are at least $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ distinct
distances?

This question has been answered negatively by Xichuan in the
[comments](https://www.erdosproblems.com/forum/thread/1082), who gave a set of $42$ points in
$\mathbb{R}^2$, with no three on a line, such that each point determines only $20$ distinct distances.

A smaller counterexample has been formalised here: it comprised of $8$ points, where each point only
determines $3$ distances.

This counterexample has originally been found by Heiko Harborth.
statement:
False ↔
  ∀ (A : Finset (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 2))),
    A.Nonempty →
      EuclideanGeometry.NonTrilinear ↑A →
        ∃ a, ∃ (_ : a ∈ A), A.card / 2 ≤ EuclideanGeometry.distinctDistancesFrom A a - 1

docstring:
A folklore result states that any $a_n$ satisfying $\lim_{n \to \infty} a_n^{\frac{1}{2^n}} = \infty$
has $\sum \frac{1}{a_n}$ converging to an irrational number.
statement:
∀ (a : ℕ → ℕ),
  Filter.Tendsto (fun n => ↑(a n) ^ (1 / 2 ^ n)) Filter.atTop Filter.atTop → Irrational (∑' (n : ℕ), 1 / ↑(a n))

docstring:
Must every irrationality sequence $a_n$ in the above sense
satisfy $a_n^{1/n} \to \infty$ as $n \to \infty$? 
Answer: false.
statement:
False ↔
  ∀ (a : ℕ → ℕ),
    Erdos263.IsIrrationalitySequence a → Filter.Tendsto (fun n => ↑(a n) ^ (1 / ↑n)) Filter.atTop Filter.atTop

docstring:
Kovač and Tao [KoTa24] proved that any strictly increasing sequence $a_n$ such that
$\sum \frac{1}{a_n}$ converges and $\lim \frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n^2} = 0$ is not
an irrationality sequence in the above sense.

[KoTa24] Kovač, V. and Tao T., On several irrationality problems for Ahmes series.
         arXiv:2406.17593 (2024).
statement:
∀ (a : ℕ → ℕ),
  StrictMono a →
    (Summable fun n => 1 / ↑(a n)) →
      Filter.Tendsto (fun n => ↑(a (n + 1)) / ↑(a n) ^ 2) Filter.atTop (nhds 0) → ¬Erdos263.IsIrrationalitySequence a

docstring:
On the other hand, if there exists some $\varepsilon > 0$ such that $a_n$ satisfies
$\liminf \frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n^{2+\varepsilon}} > 0$, then $a_n$ is an irrationality sequence
by the above folklore result `erdos_263.variants.folklore`.
statement:
∀ (a : ℕ → ℕ),
  (∀ (n : ℕ), a n > 0) →
    StrictMono a →
      (∃ ε > 0, Filter.liminf (fun n => ↑(a (n + 1)) / ↑(a n) ^ (2 + ε)) Filter.atTop > 0) →
        Erdos263.IsIrrationalitySequence a

docstring:
Koizumi [Ko25] showed that $a_n = \lfloor \alpha^{2^n} \rfloor$ is an irrationality sequence
for all but countably many $\alpha > 1$.

[Ko25] Koizumi, J., Irrationality of the reciprocal sum of doubly exponential sequences,
       arXiv:2504.05933 (2025).
statement: ∀ᶠ (α : ℝ) in Filter.cocountable, α > 1 → Erdos263.IsIrrationalitySequence fun n => ⌊α ^ 2 ^ n⌋₊

docstring: Is $a_n = 2^{2^n}$ an irrationality sequence in the above sense?
statement: True ↔ Erdos263.IsIrrationalitySequence fun n => 2 ^ 2 ^ n

docstring: Every triangle is cuttable into any non-zero square number of congruent triangles.
statement: ∀ {n : ℕ} {T : Affine.Triangle ℝ (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 2))}, n ≠ 0 → IsSquare n → Erdos633.IsCuttable n T

docstring: A triangle isn't simili-cuttable into zero triangles.
statement: ∀ {n : ℕ} {T : Affine.Triangle ℝ (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 2))}, Erdos633.IsSimiliCuttable n T → n ≠ 0

docstring:
A triangle whose side lengths and angles are integrally independent is cuttable only into
a non-zero square number of congruent triangles. This is proved in [So09c].
statement:
∀ {n : ℕ} {T : Affine.Triangle ℝ (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 2))},
  LinearIndependent ℤ
      ![dist (T.points 0) (T.points 1), dist (T.points 1) (T.points 2), dist (T.points 2) (T.points 0)] →
    LinearIndependent ℤ
        ![EuclideanGeometry.angle (T.points 0) (T.points 1) (T.points 2),
          EuclideanGeometry.angle (T.points 1) (T.points 2) (T.points 0),
          EuclideanGeometry.angle (T.points 2) (T.points 0) (T.points 1)] →
      (Erdos633.IsCuttable n T ↔ n ≠ 0 ∧ IsSquare n)

docstring: Which triangles can only be decomposed into a square number of congruent triangles?
statement: ∀ {T : Affine.Triangle ℝ (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 2))}, T ∈ sorry ↔ ∀ (n : ℕ), Erdos633.IsCuttable n T → IsSquare n

docstring:
There exists a triangle which isn't simili-cuttable into 0, 2, 3, 5 parts.
This is proved in [So09].
statement: ∃ T, ∀ (n : ℕ), Erdos633.IsSimiliCuttable n T ↔ n ≠ 0 ∧ n ≠ 2 ∧ n ≠ 3 ∧ n ≠ 5

docstring:
Every triangle is simili-cuttable into any number of similar triangles, except 0, 2, 3, 5.
This is proved in [So09].
statement:
∀ {n : ℕ} {T : Affine.Triangle ℝ (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 2))},
  n ≠ 0 → n ≠ 2 → n ≠ 3 → n ≠ 5 → Erdos633.IsSimiliCuttable n T

docstring: Every triangle is cuttable into any non-zero square number of congruent triangles.
statement: ∀ {n : ℕ} {T : Affine.Triangle ℝ (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 2))}, n ≠ 0 → Erdos633.IsCuttable (n ^ 2) T

docstring: A triangle isn't cuttable into zero triangles.
statement: ∀ {n : ℕ} {T : Affine.Triangle ℝ (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 2))}, Erdos633.IsCuttable n T → n ≠ 0

docstring:
Let $A \subset \mathbb{N}$ be an additive basis of order 2.

Must there exist $B = \{b_1 < b_2 < \dots\} \subseteq A$ which is also a basis such that
$\lim_{k\to\infty} \frac{b_k}{k^2}$ does not exist?
statement:
True ↔
  ∀ (A : Set ℕ),
    A.IsAddBasisOfOrder 2 →
      ∃ b,
        StrictMono b ∧
          ∀ (n : ℕ),
            b n ∈ A ∧
              (Set.range b).IsAddBasis ∧ ∀ (x : ℝ), ¬Filter.Tendsto (fun n => ↑(b n) / ↑n ^ 2) Filter.atTop (nhds x)

docstring: Erdős originally asked whether this was true with `A = B`, but this was disproved by Cassels.
statement:
∃ a,
  ∃ (_ : StrictMono a) (_ : (Set.range a).IsAddBasisOfOrder 2),
    ∃ x, ∃ (_ : 0 < x), Filter.Tendsto (fun n => ↑(a n) / ↑n ^ 2) Filter.atTop (nhds x)

docstring:
An example of an $A$ with the property that there are no distinct $a,b,c \in A$ such that
$a \mid (b+c)$ and $b,c > a$ and such that
$$\liminf \frac{\lvert A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert}{N^{1/2}}\log N > 0$$
is given by the set of $p^2$, where $p\equiv 3\pmod{4}$ is prime.
statement:
∀ (A : Set ℕ),
  A = {x | ∃ p, ∃ (_ : Nat.Prime p) (_ : p ≡ 3 [MOD 4]), p ^ 2 = x} →
    Erdos12.IsGood A ∧ 0 < Filter.liminf (fun N => ↑(A ∩ Set.Icc 1 N).ncard * Real.log ↑N / √↑N) Filter.atTop

docstring:
The set of $p ^ 2$ where $p \cong 3 \mod 4$ is prime is an example of a good set.
Formal proof provided by AlphaProof
statement: Erdos12.IsGood {x | ∃ p, ∃ (_ : p ≡ 3 [MOD 4]) (_ : Nat.Prime p), p ^ 2 = x}

docstring:
Erdős and Sárközy proved that such an $A$ must have density 0.
[ErSa70] Erd\H os, P. and Sárk\"ozi, A., On the divisibility properties of sequences of integers.
    Proc. London Math. Soc. (3) (1970), 97-101
statement: ∀ (A : Set ℕ), Erdos12.IsGood A → A.HasDensity 0

docstring:
Let $A$ be a set of natural numbers with the property that there are no distinct $a,b,c \in A$ such
that $a \mid (b+c)$ and $b,c > a$. If all elements in $A$ are pairwise coprime then
$$\lvert A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert \ll N^{2/3}/\log N$$
statement:
∀ (A : Set ℕ),
  Erdos12.IsGood A →
    A.Pairwise Nat.Coprime → (fun N => ↑(A ∩ Set.Icc 1 N).ncard) =O[Filter.atTop] fun N => ↑N ^ (2 / 3) / Real.log ↑N

docstring:
Given any function $f(x)\to \infty$ as $x\to \infty$ there exists a set $A$ with the property
that there are no distinct $a,b,c \in A$ such that $a \mid (b+c)$ and $b,c > a$, such that there are
infinitely many $N$ such that $$\lvert A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert > \frac{N}{f(N)}.
statement:
∀ (f : ℕ → ℕ),
  Filter.Tendsto f Filter.atTop Filter.atTop →
    ∃ A, Erdos12.IsGood A ∧ {N | ↑N / ↑(f N) < ↑(A ∩ Set.Icc 1 N).ncard}.Infinite

docstring:
Let $A$ be a set of natural numbers with the property that there are no distinct $a,b,c \in A$ such
that $a \mid (b+c)$ and $b,c > a$. If all elements in $A$ are pairwise coprime then
$$\lvert A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert \ll N^{2/3}$$
statement:
∀ (A : Set ℕ),
  Erdos12.IsGood A → A.Pairwise Nat.Coprime → (fun N => ↑(A ∩ Set.Icc 1 N).ncard) =O[Filter.atTop] fun N => ↑N ^ (2 / 3)

docstring:
Let $A$ be an infinite set such that there are no distinct $a,b,c \in A$
such that $a \mid (b+c)$ and $b,c > a$. Does there exist some absolute constant $c > 0$
such that there are always infinitely many $N$
with $|A \cap \{1, \dotsc, N\}| < N^{1−c}$?

The DeepMind prover agent has found a formal disproof of this statement.
statement: False ↔ ∃ c > 0, ∀ (A : Set ℕ), Erdos12.IsGood A → {N | ↑(A ∩ Set.Icc 1 N).ncard < ↑N ^ (1 - c)}.Infinite

docstring:
Let $A$ be an infinite set such that there are no distinct $a,b,c \in A$
such that $a \mid (b+c)$ and $b,c > a$. Is it true that $∑_{n \in A} \frac{1}{n} < \infty$?
statement: True ↔ ∀ (A : Set ℕ), Erdos12.IsGood A → Summable fun n => 1 / ↑↑n

docstring:
Let $A$ be an infinite set such that there are no distinct $a,b,c \in A$
such that $a \mid (b+c)$ and $b,c > a$. Is there such an $A$ with
$\liminf \frac{|A \cap \{1, \dotsc, N\}|}{N^{1/2}} > 0$ ?

The DeepMind prover agent has found a formal proof of this statement.
statement: True ↔ ∃ A, Erdos12.IsGood A ∧ 0 < Filter.liminf (fun N => ↑(A ∩ Set.Icc 1 N).ncard / √↑N) Filter.atTop

docstring:
Is it true that, for every integer $t\geq1$, there is some integer $a$ such that ${n \choose k} = a$
with $1\leq k \le \frac{n}{2}$ has exactly $t$ solutions?
statement: True ↔ ∀ t ≥ 1, ∃ a, {n | ∃ k ≥ 1, 2 * k ≤ n ∧ n.choose k = a}.ncard = t

docstring:
If a finite system of $r$ congruences $\{ a_i\pmod{n_i} : 1\leq i\leq r\}$ (the $n_i$ are not
necessarily distinct) covers $2^r$ consecutive integers then it covers all integers.

This is best possible as the system $2^{i-1}\pmod{2^i}$ shows. This was proved independently by
Selfridge and Crittenden and Vanden Eynden [CrVE70].

This was formalized in Lean by Alexeev using Aristotle.
statement:
∀ (r : ℕ) (a : Fin r → ℤ) (n : Fin r → ℕ),
  (∃ k, ∀ x ∈ Set.Ico k (k + 2 ^ r), ∃ i, x ≡ a i [ZMOD ↑(n i)]) → ∀ (x : ℤ), ∃ i, x ≡ a i [ZMOD ↑(n i)]

docstring:
Does there exist a minimal basis $A \subset \mathbb{N}$ with positive density
such that, for any $n \in A$, the (upper) density of integers which
cannot be represented without using $n$ is positive?
statement:
True ↔
  ∃ A h,
    Erdos330.MinAsymptoticAddBasisOfOrder A h ∧ A.HasPosDensity ∧ ∀ n ∈ A, (Erdos330.UnrepWithout A n h).HasPosDensity

docstring: According to https://www.erdosproblems.com/672, Euler proved this.
statement: Erdos672.Erdos672With 4 2

docstring:
Can the product of an arithmetic progression of positive integers $n, n + d, ..., n + (k - 1)d$
of length ≥ 4, with $(n, d) = 1$, be a perfect power?
statement: True ↔ ∀ (k l : ℕ), l > 1 → k ≥ 4 → Erdos672.Erdos672With k l

docstring:
According to https://www.erdosproblems.com/672, Obláth proved this.

[Ob51] Oblath, Richard, Eine Bemerkung über Produkte aufeinander folgender Zahlen.
J. Indian Math. Soc. (N.S.) (1951), 135-139.

docstring:
For all $n\ge 2k$ the least prime factor of $\binom{n}{k}$ is $\le\max(n/k,k)$, with only
finitely many exceptions.
statement: {(n, k) | 0 < k ∧ 2 * k ≤ n ∧ (n.choose k).minFac > max (n / k) k}.Finite

docstring:
Is $\sum_{n} \mu(n)^2\frac{n}{2^n}$ irrational?

This is true, and was proved by Chen and Ruzsa.

[ChRu99] Chen, Yong-Gao and Ruzsa, Imre Z., On the irrationality of certain series. Period. Math. Hungar. (1999), 31--37.
statement: Irrational (∑' (n : ℕ), ↑(ArithmeticFunction.moebius n) ^ 2 * ↑n / 2 ^ n)

docstring:
Let $f$ be a Rademacher multiplicative function.
Does there exist some constant $c > 0$ such that, almost surely,
$$
  \limsup_{N \to \infty} \frac{\sum_{m \leq N} f(m)}{\sqrt{N \log \log N}} = c?
$$
statement:
∀ {Ω : Type u_1} [inst : MeasureTheory.MeasureSpace Ω] [MeasureTheory.IsProbabilityMeasure MeasureTheory.volume],
  True ↔
    ∃ c > 0,
      ∀ (f : ℕ → Ω → ℝ),
        Erdos520.IsRademacherMultiplicative f →
          ∀ᵐ (ω : Ω),
            Filter.limsup (fun N => ∑ m ∈ Finset.Iic N, f m ω / √(↑N * Real.log (Real.log ↑N))) Filter.atTop = c

docstring: Sanity Check: the trivial ruler is actually a perfect ruler if $K \geq N$
statement: ∀ (N : ℕ), Erdos170.TrivialRuler N ∈ Erdos170.PerfectRulersLengthN N

docstring:
The existence of the limit has been proved by Erdős and Gál [ErGa48].
The lower bound has been proven by Leech [Le56], who refined an argument of Rédei and Rényi.
The upper bound is due to Wichmann [Wi63].
statement:
∃ x ∈ Set.Icc Erdos170.lower_bound Erdos170.upper_bound,
  Filter.Tendsto (fun N => ↑(Erdos170.F N) / √↑N) Filter.atTop (nhds x)

docstring: The problem is to determine the limit of the sequence $\frac{F(N)}{\sqrt{N}}$ as $N \to \infty$.
statement: Filter.Tendsto (fun N => ↑(Erdos170.F N) / √↑N) Filter.atTop (nhds sorry)

docstring:
Let $A=\{1\leq a_1 < a_2 < \cdots\}$ and $B=\{1\leq b_1 < b_2 < \cdots\}$ be sets of integers with
$a_n/b_n\to 1$.

If $A+B$ contains all sufficiently large positive integers then is it true that
$\limsup 1_A\ast 1_B(n)=\infty$?

A conjecture of Erdős and Sárközy.
statement: True ↔ Erdos1145.Erdos1145Prop

docstring: A stronger form of [erdosproblems.com/28].
statement:
Erdos1145.Erdos1145Prop →
  ∀ (A : Set ℕ), (A + A)ᶜ.Finite → Filter.limsup (fun n => ↑(AdditiveCombinatorics.sumRep A n)) Filter.atTop = ⊤

docstring:
If $A ⊆ \mathbb{N}$ is such that $A + A$ contains all but finitely many integers then
$\limsup 1_A ∗ 1_A(n) = \infty$.
statement: ∀ (A : Set ℕ), (A + A)ᶜ.Finite → Filter.limsup (fun n => ↑(AdditiveCombinatorics.sumRep A n)) Filter.atTop = ⊤

docstring:
Let $A = \{a_1 < a_2 < \dots\} \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ and let $F(A,X,k)$ count the number of $i$
such that $[a_i,a_{i+1}, \dots ,a_{i+k−1}] < X$, where the left-hand side is the least common
multiple. Is it true that, for every $\epsilon > 0$, there exists some $k$ such that
$F(A,X,k) < X^\epsilon$?
statement: True ↔ ∀ (a : ℕ → ℕ), ∀ ε > 0, 0 < a 0 → StrictMono a → ∃ k, ∀ X > 0, ↑↑(Erdos873.F a X k) < ↑(X ^ ε)

docstring: Is $n! - 1$ powerful for finitely many $n$?
statement: True ↔ Erdos936.EventuallyNotPowerful fun x => x.factorial - 1

statement: True ↔ Erdos936.EventuallyNotPowerful fun x => x.factorial + 1

docstring:
**Erdős Problem 598:**
Let $m$ be an infinite cardinal and $\kappa$ be the successor cardinal of $2^{\aleph_0}$.
Can one colour the countable subsets of $m$ using $\kappa$ many colours so that every
$X \subseteq m$ with $|X| = \kappa$ contains subsets of all possible colours?
statement: ∀ (m : Type u_1) [Infinite m], True ↔ ∃ c, ∀ (X : Set m), Cardinal.mk ↑X = Erdos598.κ → c '' {s | ↑s ⊆ X} = Set.univ

docstring:
This lemma confirms that the set of possible unit distance counts is bounded above, which
ensures that taking the supremum (`sSup`) is a well-defined operation. The trivial upper bound is
the total number of pairs of points, $\binom{n}{2}$.

docstring:
Upper bound (Davies–Illingworth 2022).
There exists a constant $c_2 \ge 2$ such that, for sufficiently large $n$,
$$
f(n) \le c_2 \sqrt{\frac{n}{\log n}},
$$
where $f(n)$ denotes the maximum chromatic number of a triangle-free graph on
$n$ vertices, formalized as `triangleFreeMaxChromatic n`.
statement: ∃ c₂, 2 ≤ c₂ ∧ ∀ᶠ (n : ℕ) in Filter.atTop, ↑(Erdos1104.triangleFreeMaxChromatic n) ≤ c₂ * √↑n / √(Real.log ↑n)

There exists a constant $c_1 \in (0,1]$ such that, for sufficiently large $n$,
$$
c_1 \sqrt{\frac{n}{\log n}} \le f(n),
$$
where $f(n)$ denotes the maximum chromatic number of a triangle-free graph on
$n$ vertices, formalized as `triangleFreeMaxChromatic n`.
statement: ∃ c₁, 0 < c₁ ∧ c₁ ≤ 1 ∧ ∀ᶠ (n : ℕ) in Filter.atTop, c₁ * √↑n / √(Real.log ↑n) ≤ ↑(Erdos1104.triangleFreeMaxChromatic n)

docstring:

$$

docstring:
Tao observed that `erdos_69` is a special case of `erdos_257`, since
$$
\sum_{n\geq 2}\frac{\omega(n)}{2^n} = \sum_p \frac{1}{2^p - 1}.

have A := {n | Nat.Prime n};

docstring:
**Erdős–Herzog–Piranian Component Lemma** (Metric Properties of Polynomials, 1958):
If $f$ is a monic degree $n$ polynomial with all roots in the unit disk,
then some connected component
of $\{z \mid |f(z)| < 1\}$ contains at least two roots with multiplicity.

See p. 139, above Problem 5:
[EHP58] Erdős, P. and Herzog, F. and Piranian, G., _Metric properties of polynomials_.
  J. Analyse Math. (1958), 125-148.
statement:
∀ (n : ℕ) (f : Polynomial ℂ),
  n ≥ 2 →
    f.natDegree = n →
      f.Monic →
        f.rootSet ℂ ⊆ Metric.ball 0 1 →
          ∃ C ⊆ {z | ‖Polynomial.eval z f‖ < 1}, IsConnected C ∧ 2 ≤ (Multiset.filter (fun x => x ∈ C) f.roots).card

docstring:
Let
$$ f(z) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} (z - z_i) \in \mathbb{C}[x] $$
with $|z_i| < 1$ for all $i$.

Conjecture: Must there always exist a path of length less than 2 in
$$ \{ z \in \mathbb{C} \mid |f(z)| < 1 \} $$
which connects two of the roots of $f$?
statement:
∀ (n : ℕ) (f : Polynomial ℂ),
  n ≥ 2 →
    f.natDegree = n →
      f.Monic →
        f.rootSet ℂ ⊆ Metric.ball 0 1 →
          ∃ z₁ z₂,
            ∃ (_ : {z₁, z₂} ≤ f.roots),
              ∃ γ, Set.range ⇑γ ⊆ {z | ‖Polynomial.eval z f‖ < 1} ∧ Erdos1041.length (Set.range ⇑γ) < 2

docstring:

there are distinct $a,b\in A$ such that $a+b\in A$, which establishes the $k=2$ case.

docstring:

such that (for large enough $N$) $f_k(N)\leq \left(\frac{2}{3}-\epsilon_k\right)N$.

docstring:
There exists a constant $C>0$ such that, for all large $N$, if $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,N\}$ has
size at least $\frac{5}{8}N+C$ then there are distinct $a,b,c\in A$ such that $a+b,a+c,b+c\in A$.

A problem of Erdős and Sós (also earlier considered by Choi, Erdős, and Szemerédi [CES75], but Erdős
had forgotten this).
statement:
∃ C > 0,
  ∀ᶠ (N : ℕ) in Filter.atTop,
    ∀ A ⊆ Finset.Icc 1 N,
      ↑A.card ≥ 5 / 8 * ↑N + C → ∃ a ∈ A, ∃ b ∈ A, ∃ c ∈ A, a ≠ b ∧ a ≠ c ∧ b ≠ c ∧ a + b ∈ A ∧ a + c ∈ A ∧ b + c ∈ A

docstring:
Erdős and Sós conjectured that

where $f_k(N)$ is the minimal size of a subset of $\{1, \dots, N\}$ guaranteeing $k$ elements
have all pairwise sums in the set.
statement:

  2 ≤ k →
    Asymptotics.IsEquivalent Filter.atTop (fun N => ↑(Erdos865.f N k)) fun N =>
      1 / 2 * (1 + ∑ r ∈ Finset.Icc 1 (k - 2), (1 / 4) ^ r) * ↑N

docstring:
Let $\epsilon>0$ and $N$ be sufficiently large. Is it true that if $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,N\}$ has
size at least $\epsilon N$ then there must be distinct $a,b,c\in A$ such that
$$[a, b]=[b, c]=[a, c],$$
where $[\cdot, \cdot]$ denotes the least common multiple?
statement:
True ↔
  ∀ ε > 0,
    ∀ᶠ (N : ℕ) in Filter.atTop,
      ∀ A ⊆ Finset.Icc 1 N,
        ε * ↑N ≤ ↑A.card → ∃ a ∈ A, ∃ b ∈ A, ∃ c ∈ A, {a, b, c}.card = 3 ∧ a.lcm b = b.lcm c ∧ b.lcm c = a.lcm c

docstring:
If $\mathbb{R}^2$ is finitely coloured then must there exist some colour class which contains the
vertices of a rectangle of every area?

Graham, "On Partitions of 𝔼ⁿ", Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series A 28, 89-91 (1980).
(See "Concluding Remarks" on page 96.)

Solved (with answer `False`, as formalised below) in:
Vjekoslav Kovač, "Coloring and density theorems for configurations of a given volume", 2023
https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.09973
In fact, Kovač's colouring is even Jordan measurable (the topological boundary of each
monochromatic region is Lebesgue measurable and has measure zero).

This was formalized in Lean by Alexeev and Kovac using Aristotle.
statement:
False ↔
  Erdos189.Erdos189For
    (fun a b c d =>
      (affineSpan ℝ {a, b}).direction ⟂ (affineSpan ℝ {b, c}).direction ∧
        (affineSpan ℝ {b, c}).direction ⟂ (affineSpan ℝ {c, d}).direction ∧
          (affineSpan ℝ {c, d}).direction ⟂ (affineSpan ℝ {d, a}).direction)
    fun a b c d => dist a b * dist b c

docstring:
Let $a_1, \dots, a_p$ be (not necessarily distinct) residues modulo a prime $p$, such that there
exists some $r$ so that if $S \subseteq [p]$ is non-empty and
$$\sum_{i \in S} a_i \equiv 0 \pmod{p}$$
then $|S| = r$.

Must there be at most two distinct residues amongst the $a_i$?

This was formalized in Lean by Alexeev using Aristotle and ChatGPT.
statement:
True ↔
  ∀ (p : ℕ),
    Fact (Nat.Prime p) →
      ∀ (a : Fin p → ZMod p),
        (∃ r, ∀ (S : Finset (Fin p)), S ≠ ∅ → ∑ i ∈ S, a i = 0 → S.card = r) → (Set.range a).ncard ≤ 2

docstring:

docstring:
Let $C > 0$. Is it true that the set of integers of the form $n = b_1 + \cdots + b_t$,
with $b_1 < \cdots < b_t$, where $b_i = 2^{k_i}3^{l_i}$ for $1 \leq i\leq t$ and
$b_t \leq Cb_1$ has density $0$?

van Doorn and Everts \cite{vDEv25} have disproved this with $C=6$ - in fact, they prove that all
integers can be written as such a sum in which $b_t<6b_1$.

This was formalized in Lean by Alexeev using Aristotle.
statement:
False ↔
  ∀ (C : ℝ),
    0 < C →
      have f := fun x =>
        match x with
        | (k, l) => 2 ^ k * 3 ^ l;
      {x | ∃ B, ∃ (h : B.Nonempty) (_ : ↑(B.sup f) ≤ C * ↑(B.inf' h f)), ∑ x ∈ B, f x = x}.HasDensity 0
